Oṃ, homage to Śiva.
Having paid homage to Maheśvara, the destroyer of the bonds of worldly existence,
and to the Goddess Śakti, whose nature consists of knowledge and action, who is the consort of Śiva;
Having prostrated with supreme devotion before Nandi, Skanda, and Vināyaka,
he then bowed with devotion to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), the source of the knowledge of Śiva.
Now, for the sake of purifying evil, I shall briefly describe the expiation prescribed in the scriptures for practitioners who perform ritual actions.
For practitioners who are always engaged in the conduct of the samaya,
various accomplishments— superior, inferior, and middling— arise at all times.
Otherwise, it is not accomplished at all by transgressing the penance;
just as the fruit of agriculture must be protected from cattle and other such threats on the field.
According to the Dharma, all four must be protected equally:
the teacher, the practitioner, the spiritual son, and likewise the initiate.
Furthermore, these commitments of the knower of the rules must be protected by means of penances and other such measures;
this applies to the sacrificer who has been previously initiated.
O Samayākṣi, by the mere sight [of him], he is declared to be the son of a son, the practitioner of a practitioner, and even the teacher of a teacher.
The expiation taught by Śiva and the established dharma must be performed by all four classes of attendants (gaṇas), even those situated in the various stages of life (āśramas).
The pure conduct of the four stages of life (āśramas) is now being described: wearing matted hair, carrying a staff, shaving the head, eating only what is permitted, dwelling on the ground,
serving the teacher as one would a great deity, avoiding improper associations, and speaking the truth.
Rising at the three times of day, freedom from anger, and patience belong to the celibate practitioner.
Chanting for the sake of giving, performing oblations, honoring guests,
and being devoted to one's own wife— this is declared to be the conduct of a householder.
Performing fire rituals, dwelling in the forest, subsisting on fruits, roots, and the like, sleeping on the ground, not wearing [fine] clothing, and avoiding the acceptance of gifts.
The restraint of all the senses is the conduct of one who has reached the end of the forest;
the abandonment of all undertakings is the taking up of residence at the foot of a tree.
In the teaching, you are unshaken by pleasure or pain;
you are established in meditation, with that very essence both internal and external.
The renunciation of the pleasant and the unpleasant is declared to be the conduct of an ascetic;
one should practice the Śaiva conduct as prescribed in the scriptures and spoken by the Great Lord.
Otherwise, a fall is declared to result from transgressing the conduct of the observance (samaya). I shall now proclaim those observances as they were revealed by the God of gods.
One should always carry out the command of the guru through action, mind, and speech;
in his presence, one should certainly not engage in self-censure nor in censure of him.
One should avoid reciting scriptures, singing, dancing, and erotic displays.
One should not engage in jesting in the presence of the guru, the gods, fire, or a brahmin. Furthermore, one should avoid voiding excrement, urine, spitting, yawning, and sneezing in that place.
One should avoid oil massages, dry rubbing with powders, and shaving with a razor;
furthermore, one must never engage in the censure of those devoted to the practice of mantras.
May he abandon mental derangement, negligence, sensual desire, anger, recklessness, doubt, hostility toward others, evil association, and hypocrisy.
One should avoid agitation, lack of enthusiasm, nihilism, confusion, weakness, hardness, as well as delusion and worldly involvement.
Likewise, for one who possesses fearlessness, all ritual actions are effective means;
he should not criticize the deity even when there is a reason, nor should he disparage the words originating from Him.

One should avoid a linga that is devoid of other principles, as well as its shadow and so forth; likewise, one should avoid what has been touched by a corpse during the seasons of death, and what is overcooked or otherwise spoiled.
Having cleansed the property of the God of gods, one should cause it to be immersed during the festival procession (*yātrā*).
One must not employ the property of the deity, the property of the guru, or any other such property for any other purpose.
Avoiding negligence, it should be protected with great effort.
One should cause even the pure rites for the Guru and the deities to be performed.

A wise person should not desire the fruit of that [action], nor should they engage in various undertakings and activities as long as Śaṅkara has not been worshipped; one should not perform any rite until he has been honored.
Those devoted to Śiva should be viewed as Śiva himself by those who desire Śiva;
they must always be protected from fear, poverty, and passion.
In no way should one go outside of the *svatikā* (the protective enclosure),
lest there be a loss of the vow.
p. 3a) For those who are devotees of Rudra, the mantra for eating is proclaimed.
A person of good character and one belonging to an āśrama—namely, a student (brahmacārī) or a householder (gṛhastha)—should be fed.
The end of the counsel between the king and his minister is not to be disclosed; likewise, one should not perform recitation (*japa*) for those who follow other sectarian marks (*liṅgin*).
For all self-controlled persons, however, the recitation is prescribed everywhere at the rate of one thousand repetitions.
Having performed the ritual in water reaching only to the knees and having restrained the stream of the senses,
purity thus arises through the sounds and other means taught by the Guru.
Thus ends the chapter on the listener in the general section of the Pārameśvara Mahātantra.
The Supreme Lord said:
Sadyojāta is in the midst of cows; Vāmadeva is in the abode of Śiva;
Bahurūpa is in the great cremation ground; and the face [Aghora] is in the abode of the three fires.
On Mount Kedāra, one should always perform expiation;
having intentionally killed a cow, one should practice the Vāmadeva mantra.
Having stolen gold, the wise man should mutter the Bahurūpa mantra.
Having approached the body of a guru or the body of a serpent out of negligence, one should recite the *puruṣasūkta*. Due to association with these four types of fallen persons, [one becomes impure].
And indeed, one hundred thousand [times]; and according to one's desire, one should likewise rotate the hundred thousand.
A wise person should mutter the *Brahma-mantra* a thousand times in secret; [this applies] when there is the emission of semen, feces, or urine, or when these have been consumed.
By reciting the Vāmadeva hymn one hundred times, one is liberated from that sin—
whatever action has been conceived, whether born of an egg, born of a womb, or otherwise.
Having taken hold of a hide, the wise man should recite the Sadyojāta mantra;
likewise, [he should offer] ghee, milk, curd, honey, oil, and salt.
Having taken sugar-candy, jaggery, and granulated sugar, one should practice [the ritual];
likewise, having taken silver, gold, gems, and pearls.
One should recite the Vaktṛ-form from the Hīna[-tantra], as well as the Dhenu[-mantra].
One should recite the Tatpuruṣa[-mantra] from the Siddha[-tantra], having taken hold of the woman herself.
Those who are liberated from all sins and who uphold the knowledge of Śiva;
The expiation has been proclaimed for the sake of preserving worldly convention.
Thus ends the third chapter on expiation in the *Puṣkara*, the great tantra of the Supreme Lord, which is a general compendium.
Brahmā said:
What is said to be the "middle of the cow," and what is said to be the "abode of Śiva"?
O God, what is remembered as the "cremation ground," and what is the "house of the fire-sacrifice"?
"O Lord of Gods, you ought to tell me in truth what the summit of the mountain is.
The Supreme Lord said:
The middle of a cow-pen is equal to a thousand elephants;
O Brahmin, a cow-pen smaller than a thousand is said to be common.
The *gomadhyam* is declared to be the *maṇḍala*, and the three *saurabheyas* are remembered [therein]; likewise, there is the *ṛṣabha* and the *dhenu-maṇḍala*.
O Brahmin, there eleven fragrant cows are worshipped along with their calves: eight are situated in the cardinal directions, and three are in the center of the mandala.
And in the middle of their noses, the Bull himself is established;
the goddesses are in the state of the wish-fulfilling cow, consisting of that very essence for the sake of the gods.
The maṇḍala should be eight cubits in size and divided into nine or ten sections;
it is square, with four gates, four colors, and is beautiful to behold.
At the conclusion of the recitation, those who know the reality, established in the ritual of Sadyojāta,
desire either great supernatural power or liberation from which there is no return.
Thus, in the *Puṣkarapārameśvara-mahātantra*, in the section on general matters, is the verse concerning the midst of the cow;
in the *Śrīpuṣkarapārameśvara*, this is the fifth method of ritual procedure:
with *sadyojāta* one takes cow urine, and with *vāmadeva* one takes cow dung.
One should take milk with the Bahurūpa mantra, curd with the Tatpuruṣa mantra,
clarified butter with the Īśāna mantra, and water with kuśa grass with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Then, by means of the deity who is the self of all, one should contemplate [the mantra] as being situated in one place:
*oṃ kāmantra he svāhā*.
Oṃ jagadyoni svāhā! Vaiṣṇavī is in the north. Oṃ amoghamātre svāhā!

The Bull is between the two. *Oṃ jagaddhṛdaye svāhā*—Aindrī in the east (*prācyāṃ*). *Oṃ jagaddhite svāhā*—Āgneyī in the southeast (*āgneyyāṃ*). *Oṃ amṛte svāhā*—Yāmī in the south (*dakṣiṇasyāṃ*). *Oṃ namo mālinaṃ svāhā*—Nairṛtī in the southwest (*naiṛtyāṃ*). *Oṃ*...

Jagaddhenu, svāhā! Vāruṇī in the west: Oṃ śiva śakti svāhā! Vāyavī in the northwest: Oṃ sarvalokasaṃjīvani svāhā! Kauverī in the north: Oṃ varade svāhā! Aiśānī in the northeast: Oṃ sarvatejasaṃhāriṇi sarvāmṛtasaṃhāriṇi svāhā!

Svāhā! Raudrī, seated upon a bull, flows forth. Oṃ śrava śrava, gala gala, dulu dulu, may it become nectar, svāhā! The calves belong to all [the cows]. Thus ends the Treasury of Mantras for the Dhenu-maṇḍala;
the Supreme Lord said:
Brahman, denoting the universal, is the abode of Śiva characterized by oneness;
however, the Maṇḍa is specifically declared to be the abode of Śiva.
Therein the auspicious gods, headed by Sṛṣṭi, are duly joined;
yet Mahāśiva alone stands in the center, pervading the void.
Śiva is stationed at his right side for the act of emission (sṛṣṭi),
and Śiva himself is at the left for maintenance (sthiti), while [the Goddess] is upon the seat of Śiva in the pericarp.
In the northeastern quarter of that [place] resides the Śiva named Saṃhāra;
in the east is Anugraha-Śiva, and in the north is Muktida-Śiva.
The forms of Śiva—Mukti, Mūrti, and Śiva—should be installed in the remaining directions in sequence;
however, Mahāśiva is to be understood as being present wherever the pervasive space (vyomavyāpin) resides.
One should know that Śiva, when abiding in the state of *bhava* and *āyuṣmat*, is the Śiva of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*);
and when abiding in the state of *bhavodbhava*, he is the Śiva of perpetual maintenance (*sthiti*).
Oṃ muñca muñca; Śiva, established in the state of *pada*, is known as Saṃhāra (the Withdrawal).
From Śiva down to Sarva, he should be understood as the bestower of the earth (*bhūmidah*).
The first Śiva, beginning from Tattva and ending with Śiva, is the bestower of liberation;
for there is no second Śiva who begins with you and ends with Śiva as the bestower of liberation.
The third [syllable] stands at the beginning of the pair of salutations (namaskāra) and ends with the Praṇava;
these three are proclaimed as the eyes of Śivājñyā, the embodiment of liberation.
The mandala should be fashioned as before, square in shape, according to the prescribed measurements of the cord, or else it may be pleasing to the mind.
Thus ends the section on the mandala of the abode of Śiva within the general chapter of the Puṣkara-pārameśvara-mahāmantra.
Oṃ, salutation to Vyomavyāpin; Mahāśiva. Oṃ, salutation to Bhavabhava; Sṛṣṭiśiva. Oṃ, salutation to Bhavodbhava; Sthitiśiva. Oṃ, salutation to Muñca Muñca.

Saṃhāraśiva: Oṃ, salutation to the bestower of happiness upon all beings. Anugrahaśiva: Oṃ, salutation to Śiva; Oṃ, salutation, salutation to Śiva, salutation, salutation. Muktiśiva: Oṃ, first salutation. Tirobhāvaśiva: Oṃ, salutation to the one who is everything for everyone. Bhūtidaḥ Śiva: [Salutation to] Śiva, the bestower of prosperity.

Oṃ, salutation to Śiva. Salutation to the first Mūrti-Śiva, the embodiment of liberation. Oṃ, salutation, salutation to Śiva; salutation. The second is Mūrti-Śiva. Oṃ, salutation, salutation. The third is Mūrti-Śiva, the embodiment of liberation. Thus concludes the Treasury of Mantras for the Maṇḍala of the Abode of Śiva.
The Supreme Lord said:
Wherever a cremation ground is seen, it is devoid of birth and life;
therefore, nothing such as the *karavīra* tree or others should be within a thousand [units] of it.
This mandala of particulars, which expresses the universal,
should be offered with flowers by you, O Guru, for the sake of the consecration of the two, using the [mantras] ending in *rūpa*.
Among them, Aghora is the first; the second is called Ghora;
then Ghoraghora, and likewise Sarvarudra.
These four are known as the auspicious ones of the cremation-ground maṇḍala:
Aghora is situated in the center of the lotus, while Ghora is established in the east.
Ghora and Ghoratara are situated in the southern direction, while Sarva is located in the direction of Varuṇa;
likewise, Rudra is assigned to the northern quarter within the mandala.
All [the deities] are to be worshipped as described, mounted upon the heads of four pretas;
thus concludes the cremation ground mandala.
Oṃ, obeisance to those who are not terrible; in the center of the mandala. Oṃ, obeisance to those who are not terrible; in the eastern direction.

Oṃ, salutation to those who are most terrible and more terrible than the terrible—[in the] southern [direction]. Oṃ, salutation to all, to every single one—[in the] western [direction]. Oṃ, salutation to you, to those of every form—[in the] northern [direction]. Thus ends the treasury of mantras for the cremation ground mandala.
O Brahmin, that house where the sacrificial fires are offered is called *agnihotra*; it is not so designated because of a thousand horses, for that term is a general designation.
O Brahmin, in the house of the Agnihotra, a special mandala is prescribed;
it consists of three steps for the deity Tatpuruṣa.
The specific distinction, however, is proclaimed as having the form of the three eyes of Hara;
therein resides the Gārhapatya fire, and the deity Tatpuruṣa is stationed there.
The sacrificial fire is Mahādeva, the southern abode of Rudra;
in the west resides the divine Puruṣa, the Great God, established from of old.
Rudra, the Lord of Devas, is proclaimed to be in the southern part of the mandala; he is worshipped as the Puruṣa who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the Agnihotra Maṇḍala. Oṃ, we know that Puruṣa; salutations! The Āhavanīya fire is the source of valid knowledge.
Oṃ, we meditate upon Mahādeva; salutation! [This is] the Āhavanīya fire. Oṃ, may Rudra be propitiated there; salutation! [This is] the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. Thus ends the mantra for the Agnihotra mandala.
The Supreme Lord said:
The peak of a mountain is generally proclaimed to be its *śikhara*;
that [peak] is said to be the summit (*varṣa*) of the principal mountain ranges (*kulācalas*).
This special maṇḍala is situated on the mountain peak;
Mount Meru is proclaimed as the preeminent among the mountain ranges of the continents.
And Vindhya is the lord of the principal mountain ranges; O lady of boundless power,
by virtue of the purpose of the mountains, his name consists of three syllables.
In the teaching, however, four others have been declared as preceding it;
that which is to be expressed as "the one called Śaśin" is proclaimed as the foremost.
In the midst of that, the youngest [son] is situated upon the peak of the fourth mountain; Īśāna is situated on the eastern mountain, and the preceding mountains are situated in the east.
Īśvara is prescribed for the south, Brahmā for the west, and Śiva on the northern petal; thus it is proclaimed in the maṇḍala.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the mountain peaks, in the section on general matters within the Puṣkaraparameśvara Mahātantra.
When the deity has been addressed, one should duly perform the evening rite;
and with the ring finger, one should, like a self-possessed person, cause the cow’s ghee and food to be eaten.
The wise one should perform the *Sujaya* rite of Vāmadeva eight hundred times;
[otherwise], there is contact with the leavings of another, and through negligence, equality [with them] occurs.
The intellect of Upasyuśaiva is said to belong to the Lord of his own caste;
however, the Brāhmaṇa born from Sukha has the limbs characterized by nourishment therein.
The Kṣatriya was born from the two arms, and that is remembered as his strength;
the Vaiśya was produced from the two thighs, and they know him to be the left limb.
The Śūdra was born from the feet; that which was released [from the mouth] is remembered as such.
Indeed, these castes are established under the Lord Brahmā, each according to its own station.
Those two should be recited together there by one born on earth;
for one day’s contact with a Kṣatriya, one should recite for a month upon contact with a Vaiśya.
O Vaiśya, for one day [one should perform the rite]; on the day of touch and so forth, one should mutter [the mantra].
A Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya is indeed purified from the touch of a Śūdra;
however, from the touch of one of an external caste (bāhyavarṇa), all [the castes] belonging to the [four] varṇas [are purified].
Having taken Śiva residing in the maṇḍala through the ritual of charcoal from a fire,
the extraction of Śiva born of one's own nature is proclaimed as your sacred ford (tīrtha).
With [the mantra] ending in *svāhā*, there is scattering and lifting;
having thus performed the recitation of the birth [mantra], the Guru should initiate them.

O Prajāpati, purification for one of an external caste occurs simply through contact; likewise, there is initiation (*dīkṣā*) according to the ritual manual (*kalpa*) from a guru, preceded by the elevation of one's birth.
However, when the preceptor is absent, one who understands [the ritual] himself should perform the task;
even those Brahmins who have reached the end of the three castes are eligible for initiation into Śiva.
For those of equal caste who have undergone initiation, one may, without hesitation, employ mantras as appropriate;
"castes" refers to Kṣatriyas and the others.
If a twice-born man,
having been invited, does not eat at the house of whichever caste he belongs to while avoiding their food, he would be a brahmin [in name].
Having recited that, one who has recited it in one place becomes purified...
[omitted] ...the non-universal and the piercing... [omitted] ...arose by itself. It is a square with four doors and four arms, very difficult to attain.
With a four-petalled lotus, [one should worship] the seed-syllable of Jāti;
in the center of the pericarp is the Daśāva, and first is that Tatpuruṣa.
Bahurūpa is in the south, and the deity [is] in the intermediate [direction];
Sadyojāta is in the west, while Ardhanārīśvara is traditionally taught [to be] in the north.
The Puruṣa is in the center of the pericarp, and Īśāna is situated in the eastern petal.
The remaining [deities] remain exactly as they were in the circle of the lords of the Brahmin classes;
Aghora is in the center of the pericarp, and Īśāna is on the southern petal.
And likewise the Śevas, according to their arrangement in the field within the circle of the lords of the castes:
Īśāna is in the pericarp of the lotus in the center, and [the others] on the inner petals.
And the remaining ones are situated according to their positions within the circle of the lords of the Vaiśya caste;
Sadyojāta is in the pericarp, and Īśāna is on the western petal.
The others who remain, as well as those of other castes in the circle of the lord of the Śūdras— O Lord of the Śūdra caste— at the end of the mantra, one must not eat with these other ascetics here.
Having eaten, one should recite the mantra of Śataliṅgeśvara in accordance with one's capacity.
The Lord is multiformed among those who bear the marks of wandering mendicants, as well as among the Pāśupatas; indeed, he is the mouth of those who bear the marks of Maheśvara.
Vāmadeva is remembered as the lord of those who possess the marks of authority, of those who have immediately cast off their sectarian marks, and of those who wear white and red footprints.
Likewise, the food of other ascetics (liṅgins) and the home of ascetics [is forbidden]; those who are ascetics by name only are proclaimed as persons whose food should not be eaten.
If they have eaten out of negligence, one should cause them to undergo initiation again;
then, having performed the extraction of the *liṅga*, the wise teacher himself should perform the initiation.
Whichever Lord is proclaimed as the presiding deity of a particular linga, by that [deity] the extraction of the linga and its installation should be performed through imperishable ritual action.
Whatever mandala has been proclaimed for Jātiśvara,
the mantra-practitioner should make that very same mandala for Liṅgeśvara.
The placement of the seat (āsana-nyāsa) alone is known in the mandala of the Lord of Beings;
the external placement of the seat is called its "subduing" (bādhanā).
The internal placement (antarnyāsa) has also been declared according to non-differentiation; now it is being described according to differentiation.
Thus, the internal placement is established by means of both the Brahmans and the Āsanas.
The placement (nyāsa) of all those who bear external forms should be performed according to what has been prescribed;
likewise, it should be done with their respective bearers of form and with the Brahmās in the central limb.
Īśāna is the name for all [mantras] of the head; Tatpuruṣa is the salutation for all.
Furthermore, Aghora is for the heart, and Vāmadeva and Guhya are proclaimed for the secret parts.
All mantras are proclaimed to be Brahman, whose form is unborn;
they are all subordinate to Brahman, provided one conceives them as Brahman.
Let the movement of the vehicles and other implements proceed like Śiva;
at the conclusion of the worship for all, [the rites] should be performed in sequence with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta.
One should not consume [the food] belonging to a Śaiva without knowing his conduct;
however, those who are pure in name alone as a Śaiva limb are remembered as true Śaivas.
O King, even a begging bowl made of clay does not attain purity through water alone.
When that [water] has been asked about its purity, one should purify it with wood-shavings or water.
The washing of a conch shell used for eating and its vessel should be done with buttermilk; likewise, the cleansing of wheat and sesame should then be performed with water.
The purification of silken garments is declared to be by means of water;
likewise, the purification of skins from predatory animals and those of deer is by means of cow’s urine.
The purification of vessels containing food and condiments is by washing with water;
likewise, the purification of water-vessels is constant, as well as by means of fire.
A vessel defiled by insects, water, or cats becomes pure after being rinsed seven times with clean water and also by the rite of circling it with fire.
One should abandon a vehicle that has been licked by dogs, donkeys, camels, or similar animals; indeed, a vessel that has been blown upon by the breath of a cow must be completely discarded.
Objects made of bone, horn, or wood, as well as vessels used for smelling,
become pure by being scrubbed seven times with ash and then purified by fire.
The purification of vessels that have been used for excellent food and so forth is like that of ordinary vessels;
as for abundant mantras defiled by crows and the like, they are purified simply by discarding that portion [of the substance].
Having determined that a defect in the food has occurred due to contact with someone who is impure from eating,
one should rinse the mouth, sprinkle water over the food and other items, and then serve the pure food to the people as before.
Is vomiting produced by the drying up of the phlegm through fasting?
Or is it proclaimed to be the removal of foul-smelling matter from the head?
A seat or a vehicle is not purified by earth and water;
women are pure in every respect, and a bird is pure by the act of dropping its fruit.
Speech is purified by truth, as a river is purified by its current; a Brahmin is purified by his menses, and one defiled by mind is purified by turning away from mental impurity.
All this is purified by the purification as previously described.
Thus ends the section on the fruit following the meal in the General Chapter of the *Pārameśvara Mahātantra* at Puṣkara. 7.
The Supreme Lord said:
O Brahmin, listen briefly to the purification of eating vessels,
as well as of other materials and the ritual sites for practitioners of mantra.
For all journeys and fasts, purification is required; whatever is not contradictory [to these rules] should be followed, while that which is contradictory must be avoided.
Indeed, a flower-offering (nirmālya) that has been touched immediately becomes pure through its abandonment;
likewise, the purification of things defiled by impurities is declared to be through their casting away.
One should discard feces, urine, and excrement after they have been taken up;
likewise, one should discard what has been struck by heat or sprinkled with semen.
Purity through renunciation is desired when there is blood, pus, or fat;
thereafter, purity comes from consecration through the application of mantras, clarified butter, and oblations.
Purity of water is achieved by circling it three times with a cloth;
the purification of Jātī flowers is declared in the scriptures to be like that of other substances.
By that very moment, through the sprinkling of water from the vessel and by the recollection of the earth,
all the houses became pure, and everything belonging to the servants became pure as well.
This [gift] is faultless when it is offered with a mind free from malice and is praised by speech;
it is pure, yet not to be further purified, as has been stated in due order.
But one should offer [the remainder] with diligence to the deity and to the guru.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the purification of the vessel, in the General Section of the Puṣkara-pārameśvara-mahātantra.
When the fire is being offered oblations with the Aghora mantra for all rites,
then any sinful defect arising from the sacrificer [is purified].
One may destroy sins such as the killing of a Brahmin by means of Sadyojāta;
Vāmadeva destroys the transgression committed through the drinking of liquor.
One may wipe away the sin born of stealing gold through many forms [of penance],
but a person shall burn away the sin of approaching the wife of a guru in an instant.
The great sin arising from contact with [these] things, whether collectively or individually,
may always be overcome by the offering of clarified butter (ājya-homa) along with purification.
One who causes harm to a preceptor shall suffer from consumption, leprosy, cough, and other ailments; therefore, one should always act for the preceptor's pleasure.

he should always wear white garments and use white garlands and unguents.

Or with ghee, or with sesame seeds mixed with ghee, or with milk and rice, or with *vrīhi* rice,

on Mount Pāriyātra, Mahendra, Vindhya, or Ayodhyā.
On the bank of the Gaṅgā, or at the ocean, on Śrīśaila, or on Mount Ṛkṣa;
Then, having himself brought a beautiful vessel filled with water from the ocean,

remaining there with a serene mind, he should perform the purification of the body.
Whether impelled by the practice of *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, or fasting on vegetables,
one should practice the *praṇava* through the restraint of the functions of the vital breath.
Having made a firm resolve, he [prepared] a full thousand corpses within six months; his body purified under an auspicious constellation, as indicated by the omens.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods of gods, one should perform the formal acceptance of the liṅga,
which was previously established by the sages and described in its entirety.
A wise person should resort to a perfected site that bestows success— whether it be naturally established or mentally conceived— but should avoid one frequented by Skanda, Indra, or the Mothers.
One should likewise prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) that has a progressively higher horn, or one that is naturally formed,
or else one endowed with the [proper] characteristics.

A linga facing west is considered excellent, while one facing east is traditionally regarded as most powerful.

having grasped and observed the auspicious *liṅga*, it is proclaimed as the *liṅga* itself.
One should constantly worship the mantras, which are like a bed for the body,

For all sins whatsoever,

Having constructed an archway with three bamboo poles,

The combination of the three sins is common to all, beginning with the Brahmin;

O Bird, having taken up earthly substances such as wood without the substance of fire,

one should likewise recite the mantra while taking hold of the earth, the linga, the scripture, and the master of the household.
If the consumption of forbidden food has occurred, one should recite the Guhyaka mantra one hundred times;
if done unintentionally, three hundred times; and if done intentionally, one should recite it while avoiding honey and other such substances.
One should recite [the mantra] before Śaṅkara for the removal of all sins, or before Brahman in due order;
having understood desire, one should practice either that state of desiring or the singular excellence.
If the consumption of the *nirmālya* occurs through negligence, one should recite the *aghora* mantra ten thousand times;
it is purified neither by another mantra nor by performing a sacrifice out of desire.
If one intentionally steps over the remains of offerings (nirmālya), one should likewise recite [the mantra] five hundred times;
if out of delusion, one should recite it three hundred times, and furthermore, one hundred times in secret.
If one has committed an act of censure against Śiva or even the Aṇu (the individual soul) out of negligence,
one shall become pure by reciting the name of the Lord one hundred times while remaining well-restrained.
For ten [repetitions] above and up to three hundred below, one becomes pure through bathing and japa;
beyond that, up to five hundred, fasting at night is prescribed.
That fast shall consist of many increases combined with three nights;
having understood that strength, knowledge, birth, and that which is accompanied by devotion.
Having investigated it with effort, one should bestow that which expels the teacher's hair;
otherwise, one should perform exactly what was spoken by the teacher.
In the case of union with one of an inferior caste, it should be performed as previously described.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the great tantra called the Kirīṇa.
Garuḍa said:
When sexual intercourse is committed out of desire with one of a lower caste, what indeed shall be the expiation? Tell me, O refuge of all the worlds!
The Blessed One said:
If the *mandi* star is situated in a house where the *aṅgaghna* (killer of limbs) of an unwilling [planet] resides,
a man becomes pure through purification by means of the *kṛcchra* penance and the renunciation of all his vessels.

Whether through sexual desire or consumption, purification occurs by performing the *sakṛcchra* or *atikṛcchra* penances or by reciting the *Vāmadevya* hymn; there is no other superior means for one who has acted contrary to the sacred path.
Having known this, one should then enjoy it; by that, he becomes absorbed in that [reality].
Even if touched by a washerwoman’s hide, or if [the vessel] is situated in a temple, [it remains pure].
I took five thousand coins from Bhāṇḍānvāmā and Icchaddhikhyā;
having enjoyed them through desire for those two, I shall perform a terrible *kṛcchra* penance.
Or, through desire, an action may become double in this world even from a single union;
whereas through lack of desire, there is a manifold conjunction, which arises for both of them alike.
Then the Cāndrāyaṇa penance must be performed; otherwise, one is not purified at all.
Whether it was by chance or through the power of past karma, that Devaśika conjunction has occurred.
In that case, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance must be performed with water alone;
however, for a sin consisting of violence toward living beings, purification comes through the recitation of the Śavaghora mantra.
Having thoroughly investigated and understood the tenfold form of a terrible sin arising from desire or even from passion, one should grant purification once again through the Guru.
Garuḍa said:
I shall observe a single meal for three days, and for another three days I shall be compassionate; then, having eaten only at night for three days, for three days I shall subsist on air alone.
Thus is described the difficult penance known as the Prājāpatya:
one should eat only pungent food for three days, and for three days one should subsist on milk.
Having drunk hot ghee for three days and likewise consuming only a single mouthful for three days,
this is declared the *taptakṛcchra*; now hear about the *jātikṛcchra*.
The subsisting on milk for twenty-one days is declared to be the *atikṛcchra*;
now learn of the *parāka*.
Abstaining from food for twelve days is traditionally known as the *parāka* penance;
for one who is capable, there should be an increase of one morsel [of food] every half-month, and during the dark fortnight, one should decrease it.
O Lord, the Cāndrāyaṇa rite has been proclaimed; born from water, it consists of water.
Having bathed repeatedly, one should perform recitation (japa) either inside the temple or outside.
When the ritual procedure is completed, the meal prescribed by the scriptures should be taken.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Kirī," in the Mahātantra. 15.
Garuḍa said:
O Lord, if there should be contact with the remnants of another, what then?
Has the purification of the vessel been prescribed, or has it not been so stated? Even that, O Master, has not been declared.
The Blessed One said:

If one who has been initiated is touched by someone of his own caste, he becomes pure by sipping water (ācamana). Even for one who has been initiated, if he is touched by such a person, he should sip water and recite the mantra of his own caste-lord one hundred times.
That same [penalty] applies for touching one designated as a Śūdra;
however, for touching one who has been initiated (dīkṣita), there are hundreds [of years] of fasting for one whose vision is impaired.
O bird, for others, the expiation shall be reduced by one quarter.
For the castes starting from the Brāhmaṇa, [the lords] are Puruṣa, Ghorā, Vāmā, and Jātīśā.
One should avoid contact for three nights; [otherwise] there are ten thousand [repetitions], and four [thousand] for the fifth mantra—one should recite that without hesitation.
After contact with a Cāṇḍāla, the recitation of the Kṛcchrāghora mantra must be performed;
the wise man should recite it ten thousand times as an expiation for purification.
O Bird, having understood each instance according to the nature of the contact, one must apply the appropriate expiation for it;
now hear this purification of the vessel as ordained in its own scripture.
The purification of vessels made of gold, silver, and the like is desired to be by means of water;
however, the purification of conch shells and similar objects is by means of what has been rubbed with a cloth.
The purification of bell-metal is accomplished with ash; copper is purified by acid.
I have thus declared the purification for the vessel of a Brahmin who has been fed from it while impure.
Having sprinkled it, let there be purification from doubt regarding a vessel touched by one who is impure;
the purification of gourds, bamboo vessels, and the like shall be by means of milk and water.
The purification of water-vessels consists of overturning them;
and whatever wood, such as that used for fuel and so forth, is purified by being sprinkled with water.
An earthen vessel is purified by scrubbing with cow dung, as well as by sweeping;
likewise, an eggshell, one struck by excrement and the like, or one made of bamboo or clay, should be abandoned by a woman.

The purification of the remainder is as before; a woman is purified by her menses. One should discard vessels made of clay or bamboo that have come into contact with the remains of offerings (nirmālya).

The purification of the remainder shall be as previously described; the cleansing of the cloth should be done with water. One should practice the conduct prescribed by Śiva, as declared in the scriptures and taught by the Guru.
Therefore, one must act in this manner; otherwise, there would be a failure in effort.
For the ascetic (yati), there is no fault in the daily neglect of duties pertaining to the teacher, provided it is done for the sake of the teacher.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter on expiation in the great tantra known as the Kiriṇa. || 16 ||
In the *Pratiṣṭhāpārameśvara-mahātantra*, the chapter on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is now written:
"O Great Sage, having killed a Brāhmaṇa either unintentionally or intentionally..."
One should recite the Sadyojāta mantra there; then one is liberated from sin.
Or, at a confluence, a cow-pen, or a threshing floor, one should observe the vow for one day.
O Brahmin, by performing the Sadyojāta rite, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
even after killing many, the mantra-practitioner should perform the three-day vow according to the scriptures.
One who is indifferent to worldly things and skilled in recitation shall burn away evil entirely;
by conquering [the senses] day by day, one completes the remainder of the vow and becomes purified.
Having committed an act of incest with the wife of a guru, a daughter-in-law, a daughter, or likewise a sister,
a wise man should recite the Vāmadeva mantra.
Having entered into water up to one's shoulders and standing facing the sun,
one becomes purified from sin by reciting [the mantra] entirely, whether facing upwards or downwards.
Having out of delusion consumed a woman of the Cāṇḍāla caste, or one who is discolored, or one who acts according to her own lust,
or having eaten excrement or impure matter, one should thereafter mutter the Vāmadevya hymn.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel for three days without being dejected,
one should recite [the mantra] while practicing breath control; thus, one is liberated from committed sin.
One who has stolen gold, grain, or an excellent woman,
or who has acted by force or for some motive, is freed from that sin by [confessing] "I am a minister."
For stealing gold, for [stealing] cow-grain, or when treachery against a friend has been committed,
one who has employed a mantra against Śiva shall perform the vow involving earth and wood.
If a person's knee or thigh becomes submerged in water, he should remain seated for three nights and recite the Vāmadeva mantra; thus, the practitioner is liberated from that sin.
Whether one is a killer of a cow, a murderer, a slayer of a mother, or likewise a slayer of a father—
one who performs penance should recite this terrible [mantra] according to this rule and becomes purified.
Having killed his own wife, or having committed a sin characterized by an abundance of faults through Rāma,
one is liberated from that sin by reciting the Aghora mantra eight thousand times.
Having consumed forbidden food or drunk liquor, the lowest of the twice-born should recite [the mantra] for the remainder of the day; thus he is thoroughly liberated from his sins.
If, having renounced alms-food, one should eat from a single house through negligence,
one is completely freed from that fault by reciting [the mantra] once into the mouth.
One should always eat in solitude, having abandoned conventional conduct and remaining hidden;
by reciting [the mantra] day and night with the mouth, one is liberated from defects of the mantra.
Having unintentionally killed either a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya,
one becomes purified by offering a hundred oblations with eight thousand repetitions of the Īśāna mantra.
But having killed a Śūdra through negligence, or a buffalo, camel, donkey, and so forth,
one removes that sin thoroughly by reciting the Īśāna mantra a hundred times.
If a twice-born man, through delusion or negligence, emits semen upon his mother-in-law,
he is quickly liberated from that sin by reciting the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
If there should be a violation of the vow, a lapse of the vow, or an omission of the ritual act,
one should again make it flawless by reciting the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times, according to the rule.
If one who is engaged in a desired mantra or vow should become an object of your [wrath],
he is purified immediately by reciting the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
Having specifically cut down shrubs, thickets, creepers, trees, and forests,
one shall become pure in an instant by means of exactly eight hundred recitations of the Gāyatrī.
Having killed a tiger, a lion, a deer, a dog, a horse, an elephant, or a boar and others, one should recite [the mantra] eight hundred times in the respective order.
Having killed worms, insects, moths, flies, lice, bedbugs, gadflies, and even flies, one becomes pure by a single act of purification.
One bitten by a dog is purified by reciting the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times;
one bitten by a cat or a mouse is purified by reciting it seven times.
One bitten by a jackal or a wolf is purified by [the recitation of] one hundred and eight [verses],
whereas one bitten by a crocodile or a makara is purified by a single [recitation].
Having killed one born from a flower, such as a plant, even if it be many useless things,
whether visible or invisible and subtle, one is purified simply by remembering [the transgression].
For reviling Śiva or for disparaging the mantra of Śiva,
one is thoroughly purified by reciting the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
Having utterly exterminated a king or a royal family,
one is not purified even by a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), nor indeed by a single one.
Indeed, even by killing those who revile Śiva, the Śiva-mantra, and the Śaiva conduct, one violates the fire of the covenant (samayāgni).
Once, by the planting of a weapon, one hundred thousand [arrows] were successfully discharged;
yet, even against him who might be equal to Brahmā himself, if he were to strike at Śiva...

The Ācārya, who is the supreme lord and possesses the complete limbs of Śiva’s knowledge, is to be worshipped like Śiva himself; having committed an act of disparagement toward him, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times.
Whether it be a regular initiate (samayin), oneself, or especially a spiritual son (putraka),
if one utters disparagement toward them, one is not purified even by half of that [prescribed penance].
For householders who remain within the discipline of their station, there is an expiation;
however, for those who have renounced the sacrificial fires and their families, there is no sin whatsoever.
Having killed a guide out of delusion, one who subsists on alms and remains well-composed is purified by reciting eighty-one thousand times the mantra of the eighty-one syllables.
The mantra-practitioner who commits a sin here while his breath is joined in *saṃhitā* quickly reduces all that merit to ashes by means of his power.
p.
19a) Penance should be administered as prescribed to one who is unawakened,
and the previously mentioned direction for the vow should be given by those who have mastered the mantras of Śiva.
It is equal to a thousand *tulāpuruṣa* rites, a hundred *cāndrāyaṇa* observances,
a *taptakṛcchra* and an *atikṛcchra*, and a hundred *brahmakūrca* fasts.
The fruits of bathing at all sacred fords, though they may be described as great,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of one who has muttered the Gāyatrī while smeared with holy ashes.
Whatever fruit may arise from reciting a thousand million Rudra-mantras,
that is equal to reciting the Aṅga-gāyatrī mantra one hundred times.
Oṃ, may we know Sadyojāta; may we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Ghorasvara inspire us.
Thus ends the Gāyatrī of the ashes.
Oṃ, let us know Him who endures all; let us meditate upon Him whose speech is pure; may that Śiva inspire us.
The Śiva Gāyatrī.
One should purify silver and gold with water containing cow's urine and ashes;
bell-metal with alkaline water; and cloth with tannin-rich water or the water used for washing leather.
Indeed, a wooden vessel is purified by scrubbing with cow-dung and water, as is bark;
but an earthen vessel is purified by baking, while a vessel made of metal is purified by scouring.
A vessel made of metal should be heated; having been consecrated with sprinkling, it becomes pure as before.
For one who has been away on a journey, wood from a funeral pyre, and ground, are purified by cow-dung and water.
A Brahmin who has been touched by those who are highly censured and the like becomes pure by bathing;
having washed his feet, he becomes pure from contact with others, and not otherwise.
Due to contact with the remnants of food or impurities, one should perform the previously mentioned rite;
furthermore, one should discard an earthen vessel defiled by the smearing of feces or urine.
Speech purified by truth, actions performed with sincerity,
and a mind that is pure— this is everywhere declared to be purity.
Thus concludes the purification of substances.
I shall now proclaim the expiation according to the sequence of the five Brahmans;
for the sake of purifying all sins, liberation occurs through mere remembrance.
One should recite the Sadyojāta mantra in a cow-pen, in a forest, on a mountain,
at the confluence of rivers, or even in a cremation ground or a sacred sanctuary.
At a sacred bathing place (puṇyatīrtha), subsisting on water alone and well-restrained, one who has killed a Brahmin becomes pure by reciting the *Sadyojāta* mantra ten times before Śiva.
Remaining without food for seven days while engaged in recitation,
bathing three times a day, subsisting on the five products of the cow, and wearing garments of bark.
By this rite, one may purify even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
and a killer of a cow, having become purified, should immediately recite [the mantra] five hundred times.
For those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin), this very recitation is prescribed to be performed immediately;
having bathed while angry, one should resort to a sacred place.
One is quickly liberated from the sin of killing a cow through this mantra; there is no doubt about this. By fasting for a single day, one is purified from the bite of a serpent.
Having drunk liquor unintentionally, one who has performed the Gāyatrī-homa becomes pure from the taint by reciting the Sadyojāta mantra a thousand times.
Even by eating what is unfit to be eaten, one is purified from the taint after performing it once;
however, having accepted an improper gift, one is purified immediately by twelve [repetitions].

One who has committed theft, one who speaks despicably, or one who has touched a *caṇḍāla*, is quickly released from sin by reciting [the mantra] a hundred times while performing breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
There is no need for deliberation here regarding the Sadyojāta mantra;
having transgressed the word of the Guru, one becomes merely a putraka or an ācārya.
By reciting [this] five hundred times at dawn, one is liberated from transgressing against the guru;
likewise, if one sees a bad dream during the day or at night.
Having bathed, one should then recite [the mantra] immediately; thus one shall be liberated from that sin.
He who recites at the three junctions of the day should recite the Sadyojāta [mantra] one hundred times.
O Lord, sin committed during a day and night perishes in that very instant;
however, the performance of expiation has not been proclaimed for one who is "sadyojāta" (just born).
I shall declare the Vāmadeva [mantra] for the purification of one who has killed a Kṣatriya;
having recited it eight hundred times before Śiva, [one purifies] the killing of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya.
Having prepared a seat of the five products of the cow, one is liberated from that sin;
even if one afflicted by hunger or Indra himself should consume what is unfit for consumption.
Or, by reciting the Vāsa mantra five hundred times, one is released from that sin;
having offered oblations for approaching a woman who should not be approached, one should recite the Vāmadevya hymn a hundred times.
If one who has been initiated should have sexual intercourse with a Brahmin woman or any other woman,
he is liberated from that sin by reciting the *brahman* [the Gāyatrī] one hundred and eight times.
A Kṣatriya [attains success] by reciting it two hundred times, a Vaiśya even three hundred times,
and a Śūdra by reciting Vāmadeva four hundred times before Śiva.
Having stayed there for one night, he is liberated from that evil—
he who conducts himself immortally through deed, mind, and speech.
Having recited the Vāmadeva hymn one hundred times, one is freed from that sin;
for the emission of semen out of desire or anger, one should recite the two Vāmadevas one hundred times each.
If one should, through negligence, consume semen, urine, or feces,
one is liberated from that sin by reciting the Vāmadeva [Gāyatrī] a hundred times.
Whatever alms are collected from members of the four castes,
they are purified by performing seven purificatory rites, sprinkling them with water, and then offering them.
One should not designate [the offering] as being for the sake of the Guru Śiva when intending to offer the oblation;
nor should one who desires to sleep at a crossroads, in a cremation ground, or elsewhere [perform it].
If one scatters ashes in all directions, no one can overcome him;
even one joined with secret sins and the like is purified by the Vāmadeva [mantra].
Hereafter, I shall explain the atonement with reference to Aghora:
if one who is initiated into the teaching of Śiva consumes the remains of offerings (nirmālya) belonging to the Lord.
Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred and eight times and having offered oblations into the fire,
one is purified from whatever sin has been committed through action, mind, or speech.
One should recite the *ghora* mantra seven times; thereby one is liberated from that sin.
Having killed a boneless living creature, one should recite the *ghorāṣṭaka*.
But having killed a *bahu* [animal] on the right, one should mutter that same mantra three times;
likewise, having cut five stationary objects and used them for a purpose.
One should recite the Ghoramantra one hundred and one times; thereby he shall be released from that sin.
He who, having examined his own livelihood, follows another who is destitute [of means].
Learn now the purification for one who, having been initiated, commits a sin;
if he has ever fallen through his own action and has returned [to the fold].
Having recited the Aghora mantra ten thousand times for one month before Śiva,
and having offered ten thousand oblations into the Śiva-fire, one is liberated from that sin.
He who, though initiated into the teaching of Śiva, reviles the scriptures of Śiva.
One should mutter the *ghora* mantra while performing breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*); having muttered it a hundred times, one is purified.
This applies even to one who eats the leavings of another or touches anyone at all.
By reciting the Aghora mantra one hundred and eight times, one shall be liberated from that sin;
he who recites the Aghora mantra on the eighth day of the dark fortnight is [purified] at once.
He who, having been initiated, dies at a crossroads or even at a triple junction, is liberated from all sins and becomes stainless and free from rebirth.
One should recite it ten times over; thereby one is liberated from that terrible sin.
On one side is the entire Veda, and on the other side is the Gāyatrī.
Through the Gāyatrī one attains heaven, or through the Aghora mantra, the abode of Śiva;
O Brahmin, this expiation has been prescribed by me using the Aghora mantra.
Now I shall fully explain the expiation according to the excellent tradition:
if a preceptor, out of greed for wealth, initiates a Brahmin who is truly pure.
Having bathed and become pure, the wise man should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over his face;
then, having performed the fire-rite, he is liberated from that sin.
For a Kṣatriya, it is indeed one hundred; for a Vaiśya, fifty;
and for a Śūdra, twenty recitations are prescribed, as is the case for women and the three higher castes alike.
One who has been initiated should recite [the mantra] twenty-one times for eating meat;
likewise, one who eats what is not to be eaten or speaks what should not be spoken should recite it thirty times.

In the case of reviling or slandering the guru, one should recite the Vaktra mantra one hundred times; in the case of stealing the sacrificial offering, one should recite the Anānata mantra one hundred times.
If one should consume a weapon touched by a menstruating woman,
one may be released from that sin by reciting [the mantra] seven times from the mouth through his grace.
If one who has renounced alms-food should eat it in solitude out of negligence, he should recite [the mantra] over his mouth seven times; thereby he shall be liberated from that sin.
Even if a Brahmin were to recite ten million Rudra hymns in the presence of Rudra,
they would not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit gained by reciting the Tatpuruṣa mantra just once.
The mantra-practitioner should recite [the mantra] throughout all directions; for him, no sin exists.
O Lord Īśāna, I shall now explain the sequence of the ritual procedure for atonement.
Now, if someone, through negligence caused by the provocation of poison,
should recite this Īśāna mantra even once, he who was a hater of Brahmins shall become pure.
He who, out of delusion, censures Śiva, or likewise his scripture,
is not liberated from that sin even after reciting the Īśāna-mantra eight hundred times.
He who hates the eightfold divine womb and speaks of immortality,
and he who conquers the Lord through the twenty-five principles, becomes purified.
But he who should approach a female ascetic or a Brāhmaṇī woman who destroys her family,
shall be freed from that sin by reciting the Īśāna mantra one hundred and eight times.
If one who has consumed food during a period of birth-impurity should eat it unintentionally,
he becomes purified at that very moment by reciting the Īśāna mantra twenty times.
Even if one's water has been defiled by hair, insects, or feces, or has been disturbed by anyone else,
by reciting [the mantra] even once while facing Ishana, one is liberated from that sin.
Whether one is joined with other sins or even a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin),
by reciting the mantra of Īśāna while pure and having bathed before Śiva, one becomes purified.
That best of the twice-born who eats food from a single house, or even alms-food for the sake of wealth, is liberated from all sins, just as the moon is released from Rāhu.
As many morsels as one eats, for that many one is not smeared by faults;
having fasted for a day and night, one is liberated from mortal sins.
Even one who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka), if he performs the prescribed rites for the sake of purification,
is indeed released from that sin after drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Whoever constantly recites the mantra of Īśāna during an eclipse of the moon or sun, or at the equinoxes, shall be liberated from sin.
For the killer of a cow, the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
the fruit of each one of these has been declared in sequence through the mantras.
Silver, copper, bronze, milk, and so forth—
by reciting the mantra to Īśāna twenty-five times, one is released from sin.
Having committed evil through action, mind, or speech, one who is consecrated (dīkṣita) is liberated from the accumulation of sin by reciting the Īśāna mantra even once.
He who, though initiated, should eat garlic or onions, or consume *pṛśnan* and other such bulbous roots growing from the earth; or likewise one who is a heretic (*pāṣaṇḍa*).
By reciting the mantra of Īśāna even once, one is liberated from sins;
having purified all that evil, one shall obtain the desired fruit.
He goes to the secrets taught by the gods and the wise,
and to those which have been declared among the gods and repeatedly in the treatises on dharma.
All sins indeed come to an end through these [mantras] established by Brahmā;
he who abides by these becomes capable in all ritual acts.
Whoever, having been initiated into the teaching of Śiva, recites the five Brahmans,
the sin residing in his mind perishes just like [darkness] at the rising of the sun.
Just as one who has immediately desisted from violence and is provided with food and water [is fit],
so too, O King, the outcastes (antyaja) are here to be fed when they have been excluded from their own kin.

If one has eaten the food of an outcaste, which results in a painful rebirth, or likewise if one has eaten the food of a person of terrible and great sin intentionally, one should recite [the mantra] for half the duration.
Whether a washerwoman's leather bag is dragged along or kept inside the house, its purification occurs immediately through the abandonment of the outcaste; this is known as the *sahasrikā* rite.

Having eaten from those two, one should perform the Ghorajapa penance for one day if it was unintentional; if intentional, it should be performed for twice as long. A single act of sexual union with them constitutes a twofold violation of dharma.
Oṃ, homage to Nirmālyamaṭhanātha; homage!
Eight flowers offered previously are for the purification of the *nirmālya*.
The rite should be performed by Caṇḍeśvara and indeed by the Caṇḍabrahmans;
having been filled by the Caṇḍabrahmans, the vardhanī vessel should be increased.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) starting from Sadyojāta up to Caṇḍabrahman, using the mudrās previously mentioned and the Rudra-mantras in their proper sequence.
One should place Sadyojāta in the west, Vāmadeva in the northern direction,
Aghora in the south, and Vaktra in the east.
The *liṅga* is installed facing upward; then, in due order, [one offers] incense, flowers, and so forth.
Thereafter, having installed Caṇḍeśvara and worshipped him, one should offer the *arghya* in sequence.
The removal of the floral remains (nirmālya) must be performed by Caṇḍeśvara;
[the mantra is]: Oṃ Hraṃ, obeisance to the one with matted locks as pure as the moon.
The preceptor should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon his own body with the [remnants] of the pure moon;
for the drops of the floral offering falling upon his limbs serve as a cause of purification.
Oṃ hūṃ! To the fierce one of the eye, hūṃ phaṭ!
The wise one, having arranged the fierce eye-mantra, gazes with his eyes;
by the offering of eight flowers, he enters [the state] of the used garland.
Whether done unintentionally or intentionally, no fault is found therein;
O Caṇḍeśa, water was placed upon the head by the Brahmās for the sake of longevity.
One should likewise perform the offering of the *vardhanī* vessel and the vessel for water (*arthapātra*) directly upon the *liṅga*;
this is the presentation of perfumes and flowers to the deity who has been bid farewell.

One should understand that the *nirmālya* (the remains of the offering) consists of the discarded garments and ornaments; for those performing the ritual, it lasts for three days until the conclusion of the invocation and dismissal.
One should know that as "nirmālya" when the deity has been dismissed;
it is the consecrated substance always placed upon the top of the *liṅga*, not to be consumed.
One should never dismiss a deity that has been installed by oneself or by another, nor one that is temporary; likewise, one should never remove the worshipped [deity] from atop the linga.
This should continue until another time for worship has arrived,
or as long as the worship remains upon the *liṅga* or the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
One should not even recognize it as *nirmālya*; *nirmālya* is that which has fallen from the pedestal.
One must not step over *nirmālya*, but having touched it, one should wash the hand with which it was touched.
Whatever has been prescribed for whichever [rite], that alone bestows success there;
one should perform daily the rites such as the scraping of the tortoise-shaped sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as ordained.
One should generate the fire in the hearth for the three types of occasional rites;
afterwards, when the deity has been dismissed, the ash becomes Caṇḍabhasman.
One should keep vigil for him as long as the guru-maṇḍala lasts;
once the fire has been generated and consecrated, its dismissal takes place above.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the sequence of the rules for expiation (prāyaścitta),
by performing which there shall be the destruction of even great sins.

If one has intentionally consumed the substance of a guru out of devotion, one should then recite the *ghora* mantra three hundred thousand times; likewise, an ignorant person should recite it one hundred thousand times.
By offering five hundred and seven oblations into the fire, one becomes purified;
half of that for one who associates [with such a person], and half of that again for one who merely consents to the act.
Having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times over two nights in a woman's quarters during the *pratiśaṅkara* [period],
you will indeed perceive even those others who are defiled.
Their purification shall be achieved by a thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra,
when a Śaiva ascetic, a devotee of Śiva, or likewise another [such person] has been killed.
The practitioner of mantra should perform the entire expiation as spoken by Śiva and instructed by the Guru;
it cannot be performed by many teachers in the absence of the Guru.
That which is established by the scriptures must be performed for the purification of great sins (mahāpātaka);
one should prescribe the sequence of penances for ordinary minor offenses (upapātaka) according to their specific nature.
This must be performed by oneself alone, and not by others or other people;
first, one should recite [the mantra] one million times, and then offer two hundred thousand *guḍūḍuka* oblations.
The morning bath, the worship of Śiva, and the recitation of mantras continue until they are completed;
once completed, one should observe eating only at night for three days, and likewise abstain from food for another three.
Having performed three [days] of fasting, his purification is proclaimed;
however, if done unintentionally, one should perform it for three-quarters of that time, omitting the *gaḍḍuka* fasts.
Even one who has committed a bite [of leprosy] is purified by performing that same penance;
for one desiring to bow before Śaṅkara, each quarter of the sin is removed with every step taken toward Him.
In the third or fourth [case], one should perform the penance reduced by a quarter in successive order;
this is a quarter for a fallen person, and then a quarter for a twice-born man being killed.
In that case, indeed, purification is sought through fasting for half a month;
for one who desires [the fruit], purification by rain is prescribed, while for one free from desire, half of that is ordained.
In this manner, the recitation (japa) should be performed and the sequence of the water-pots (gaḍḍuka) likewise;
through all the observances (vrata) thus undertaken, one is purified of great sins (mahāpātaka).
A person who has killed a fellow initiate (samayin) in Gaṅgāvatī should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; furthermore,
having fasted for three nights, he should offer one thousand two hundred sweetmeats (laḍḍūka).
By giving [the gift], one attains purification; or, if done unintentionally, three-quarters [of the purification is attained].
He who censures his teacher becomes pure by reciting the scripture together with him.
O Sage, even if one has committed the sin of insulting a thousand maidens or one's own preceptor’s mother, purification occurs through the recitation of the Aghora mantra.
If the property of a guru, or that of the gods, or of the fierce gaṇas, has been neglected,
or if a deposit has been made with him, and it is then [misappropriated] by thieves and others out of desire;
One who is pure should recite the Aghora mantra twenty-five thousand times;
even if a practitioner of vows is killed out of anger, death will not occur.
Upon seeing blood, the wise one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times;
or, if no blood is seen, then he becomes purified by one hundred thousand recitations.
However, one should offer one thousand guḍūḍukas to Śiva;
whether unintentionally or intentionally, purification occurs in this way alone and not otherwise.
If one intentionally touches with the foot a Guru, a Linga, or likewise a scripture after having tasted them, one should recite the Dvaya mantra ten thousand times.

If one performs six times the required number of three hundred *gaḍḍūka* recitations according to one's desire, then the practitioner becomes free from defects; otherwise, he does not deserve purification.
Having unintentionally committed an offense against the teacher’s bed, seat, vehicle, sandals, or shoes, one remains pure by performing a thousand [repetitions of a mantra].
When the wise one has understood this, he should then practice the sixfold discipline;
the practitioner of mantra should proceed with the Aghora [mantra], and then purification from sin occurs.
O Śivā, even Caṇḍeśvara, having violated the command of his guru,
attained purification by reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times and [offering] eight jars of liquor from corpses.
If one recites the mantra ten thousand times unintentionally, it amounts to a hundred *gaḍḍukas*;
having nullified that instruction, the Guru should perform a hundred thousand recitations.

When an expiation has been performed, purification occurs; for an unintentional [offense], one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times. However, in the case of the omission of daily rites—whether it be recitation, fire-oblation, worship, or the like—[one must perform the prescribed penance].
One should mutter five hundred [times] the terrible [mantra]; success is desired through desire.
A single continuous lump of earth, a stream of incense, and flies [are the signs].
They do not incur sin by unintentionally violating the rules regarding the worship of the *liṅga*,
nor those concerning the guru, the scriptures, the sacred fires, the lords of the *yakṣas*, the lords of the *nāgas*, and the *yogins*.
Just as there is no *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) for Śiva belonging to the Gaṇas, Mātṛs, Ambikā, and others,
so too [there is none] for the Guru, for that which is called Śiva, for the circumambulation, and for the rite of dismissal (*visarjana*).

In the case of a mobile linga, a quadrangle, a painting, a gem, or one made of gold—among these ten locations, there is no rule regarding *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings); otherwise, however, its removal is prohibited.

The property of the deity, the wealth of the deity, the food offering (naivedya), the offering being presented, the substance for Caṇḍa, and the remains of the offering (nirmālya)— these are proclaimed as the sixfold [categories].
One should know that a country, a region, a village, and so forth, as well as female slaves, grain, and quadrupeds, constitute the property of the gods; now hear concerning the wealth of the gods.
Clothing, ornaments, incense, auspicious substances, jewels, gems, and the like—these are designated as the property of the deity. Now, listen to the description of the food offering (naivedya).

One should understand that whatever food, edibles, meals, drinks, and so forth are prepared for the sake of the deity as an offering (naivedya), it is to be placed upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā) according to the three Vedas.
On another day, having gathered together the foodstuffs, drinks, and other offerings that have been prepared for the deity, one should sit upon a pedestal.
That substance which is mixed with the remains of offerings (nirmālya) should be known as "fierce" (caṇḍa);
one should not smell it, nor step over it, nor give it away, nor sell it.
By giving [it], one goes to the state of a flesh-eater; by eating it, one enters the state of an outcaste (mātaṅga).
By skipping [a meal] for its sake, one strives for perfection; and by smelling it, one becomes a wolf.
By touching it, however, a man becomes a woman; of this there is no doubt. Otherwise, he is surely burned and is born as a *caṇḍāla*.
When that sinful, greedy fellow sells it, he would be the most wretched of men—
he who does not know the eightfold ritual procedure for the *nirmālya*.
The preceptor, the practitioner, the spiritual son, and the initiate are thus contravened.
This concludes the chapter on expiation in the *Pratiṣṭhā* section of the *Pārameśvara Mahātantra*. 15.
The expiation according to the Devīmata is now written down.
I shall explain the specific distinction; listen with a one-pointed mind:
on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights.
One should perform worship, meditation, recitation, and fire-offerings twice as much on the full moon day,
during the sun's passage into a new sign, and during lunar or solar eclipses.
During all festival occasions, the worship should consist of five [offerings] plus one more;
and when there is a conjunction [of auspicious times], one should perform the previously mentioned rite.
One should especially offer water-pots (gaḍukas) and perform recitation (japa) and other rites;
when auspicious or inauspicious dreams are seen, one should perform worship, fire-offerings (homa), recitation, and so forth.
When there is a direct vision of the Goddess, the manifestation of Kṣatrasāla,
the falling of a meteor, or when a hero has passed away, the recitation of mantras and worship shall yield greater results.
Furthermore, yoga should be practiced and the filling of the liṅga performed with beautiful flowers, such as lotuses, blue water-lilies, and the like.
Having filled the liṅga with various divine fruits that are radiant and offered with devotion to the Goddess,
one should afterwards partake of a meal with the heroes.
Otherwise, there would be no liberation, and spiritual accomplishment would be very far off;
nor would it be achieved by those seeking the fruits of ritual action if [the rite] is performed in the absence [of the proper time], or when it is marred by calamities and the like.

O auspicious lady, the preceptor should perform double the number of recitations if the twilight rite is omitted through negligence; however, if done intentionally, it is said that four times the number must be performed.
If the interruption occurs through negligence, the *cāturmāsya* rite must be performed again;
if the interruption occurs due to lack of intelligence, one should offer oblations and then recite [the mantra] two hundred times.
If one offers oblations four times more than required due to desire, and likewise performs recitation four times more;
however, if the recitation is interrupted through negligence, one should perform an equal amount of recitation prior to that point.
If meditation is interrupted through negligence, one should resort to double the duration of meditation;
likewise, if the *liṅga* becomes loose due to negligence, whether it be fixed or movable, [one must apply double the effort].
The wise practitioner should recite the vidyā, focusing on it, either upon the pedestal or at the front of the liṅga-base;
this applies even when the liṅga is mobile, or when it has been carried off by fire, water, or thieves.
In that case, the prescribed expiation is said to be one hundred thousand recitations of the Vidyā;
however, if the Liṅga falls into water or onto solid ground, it is [the same].
Even in that case, having completed one hundred thousand recitations, one must undergo purification again;
if the rosary of three strings falls while reciting, one should recite ten thousand times.
But when the practitioner goes out or returns while overcome by sleep on this earth,
then half a hundred thousand [mantras] should be recited, and for three days he should recite ten thousand.
If one intentionally touches with the foot a deity, a guru, a scripture, or even an image, one should recite the two [mantras] ten thousand times.
According to one's desire, six times the amount of three hundred *gaḍuka* measures of the ritual substance should be prepared;
this is the offering of perfumes and flowers for the deity who has been dismissed.

One should recognize that the remains of offerings (nirmālya), as well as the garments and ornaments, are to be avoided; for those performing the rites, the ritual actions should be performed daily from the invocation until the dismissal.
One should know that to be *nirmālya* when the deity has been dismissed; that which remains constantly placed upon the top of the *liṅga* is not desired as *nirmālya*.
One should never dismiss a self-manifested (svayambhū) image or one that was installed at that very time;
nor should one ever place the deity upon the top of a consecrated liṅga.
This continues as long as no other body for worship has arrived,
or as long as the worship remains upon the liṅga or the pedestal.
One should not consider [the offering] as mere refuse once it has fallen from the pedestal;
rather, one should distinguish between the acts as heavy or light according to their specific classification.
An expiation must be granted as prescribed in the scriptures and as spoken by the Guru;
however, due to my own negligence, I have spoken those words of the Guru myself.
Just as purification occurs through what the Guru bestows upon the disciple in the case of Śiva,
so too is the Guru declared to be a meditator of a hundred thousand [mantras], whose command is everywhere unimpeded.
One who is completely free from passion and hatred, and devoid of stinginess, envy, pride, and the like,
should also give a portion [of his wealth], having considered the time, the recipient, his own age, and his resources.
For the sake of purifying others through expiation in the case of a grave offense,
one should act so that no great suffering or loss of life occurs for those people.
It should be given according to the essence of one's action, concise and well-clarified;
for it should indeed be performed by others as well—by sisters, brothers, elders, children, and loved ones.
When a threat to life has arisen, one must then provide for others;
furthermore, the elderly are tormented by old age, lamentation, disease, and mental anguish.
For them, as well as for women, it should be stated in brief;
the Guru should grant [the penance] equally, as is appropriate, for the sake of purification from a mortal sin (mahāpātaka).
One should perform the *buddhātikrama* penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) in general;
likewise for other sins, whether specifically mentioned or not.
Others become pure through recitation, fasting, and enjoyment;
but for one who is initiated, consecrated, and united with Śiva, [the offering] is deposited [into the Self].

O Lord of Men, when devotion wavers, it causes one who has just been consecrated with loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to lose all that was previously accumulated, just as one season is swiftly replaced by another.
When a kinsman goes away, whether reviled or struck, one should proceed with the thought:
"The initiation has been fulfilled"; thus indeed should one go forth as a Vaiśvara.
The wise man must perform the penance exactly as it was prescribed by the Guru for the sake of purifying his inner self.
When the expiation has been prescribed by the teacher, then [one is purified];
otherwise, they go to hell, for there can never be any other way.
Having carefully examined his disciples, he should initiate them and awaken their understanding;
for a guru who has initiated others is afflicted by the faults of those disciples as well as by his own faults.
Or, if due to being sent on an errand or through association,
a mendicant should become corrupted, one should abandon that person of evil disposition and then awaken him to that [truth].
Even if he is awakened through diligent effort, if he still does not wake up— seeing him to be devoid of discernment, one should avoid him with great care.
If a Guru, by his own will, initiates disciples who are not steadfast,
he, along with those disciples, certainly falls into hell.
The disciple may be endowed with the qualities of a disciple, but the teacher is devoid of such qualities;
yet even those who have been initiated are not liberated, and the initiator shall go to hell.
Even if the teacher is endowed with his own qualities, the initiates remain transgressors.
Those who have been initiated go to hell, while the preceptor attains the state of Śiva.
That Guru who initiates disciples who have been well-examined and protected shall go to the supreme state together with those very disciples.
In the teaching of Śiva, the examination of disciples is said to be threefold:
by means of time, by means of application, and by means of their very nature.
Having unintentionally committed an offense against the teacher's bed, seat, vehicle, sandals, or shoes, one becomes pure by performing a thousand circumambulations.
When the wise one has understood this and ascends [the path], he should then recite the mantra sixfold;
the practitioner should proceed with the Aghora mantra, and then purification from sin occurs.
O beautiful one, if he should, out of delusion, fail to touch the maiden's limbs, the fire, the sun, and even water, he too shall lie dead for five days, though pure.
Having shown contempt for those who have been initiated, one falls under the sway of anger;
the practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] five hundred times with the Aghora [mantra], and thus becomes purified.
If one uses a seat, a bed, or a vehicle belonging to a guru out of negligence,
purification occurs through unintentional contact by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times after mounting it.
If one has spoken maliciously, with double-tongued speech, or anything contradictory out of desire, one is purified by reciting the Aghora mantra six times.
One should mutter the *prāyaścitta* mantra one hundred times with the *jyeṣṭha* and other mantras, or with other great [mantras].
Having muttered them three times over for each of the groups, purification is thus declared.
