Having engaged in conversation with the Guru and been established in the [initiation] stage,
one becomes pure by reciting the Aghora mantra eight thousand times.
Furthermore, one should especially pay homage to that [teacher] and ask for forgiveness;
however, those who, out of delusion, do not bow down—having destroyed their own souls through the violation of the traditional lineage—are lost.
Even for prostitutes, purification shall occur quickly;
however, in the case of providing water-pots, one should reduce [the number of repetitions] and perform a hundredfold recitation.
Knowing that at home there is a tenfold loss [of merit], one should employ [the ritual] in this manner;
however, if the deity’s water-jars and other vessels are touched by the foot, [the rite is spoiled].
If one does not desire [the result], one should recite the mantra a hundred times; if one desires it, one should recite it ten thousand times.
If the manuscript falls from the hand, one should recite the Aghora mantra ten thousand times.
That thread should be taken down to the ground when reading a book on the floor,
or upon a seat, a bed, or a mat within the house.
The Vidyā should be recited five hundred times; according to the Kaumāra tradition, it becomes twofold.
One's own Siddhānta, when its scriptures are decayed or fallen into ruin, is restored by being saturated with clarified butter.
The fire-pit must be offered into; having made the offering, one should recite the mantra a hundred times.
Even after killing a Brahmin who is free from delusion, the practitioner may act according to his will.
O auspicious lady, this Vidyā, which wards off calamities, should be recited one hundred thousand times:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya śūlapāṇe jaha 2 daha 2 paca 2 nāśaya 2 sarvapāpaṃ bhakṣa 2 hrīṃ hrūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
It is said that when the *samaya* is violated, the *vidyā* becomes a destroyer of the *vajra*.
Having discarded [the hair] from the head, likewise from the forehead, or even from ashes, clay, or water;
when the place has become stale, one should take small portions many times due to delusion for the sake of purification.
Bathing above the navel is prescribed when there is defilement by contact with the elbow;
one should not revile Śiva, the preceptor, the scripture, or those who have been initiated.
The cows, the Vedas, and their auxiliary branches, as well as the embodied deities who have entered them—
all these are always to be honored for as long as one lives in the wooden sandals of one's own guru.
Whether in his presence or in his absence, in a house where a throne is present as if for Śiva,
if the written document should somehow fall upon the ground, it must likewise be placed upon a proper seat.
If the thread thus falls while remaining on the cloth, one may proceed auspiciously;
likewise if it falls into water or fire, or if it is abandoned during the recitation.
I shall describe the purification for those beings who have not died prematurely:
one should recite [the mantra] fifty thousand times for the *gaḍukas* and indeed five hundred thousand times.
One should recite [the mantra] for him for as long as it takes to complete the recitation;
however, through intentional renunciation, whether by entering the water or otherwise, he shall be purified.
There is no fault in falling when one has not yet reached the mount;
for those who have not yet turned back from the path are not considered to have abandoned their task once they have set out.
One should practice even on a great highway or in a terrifying place;
for the sake of those who are sluggish, there is no characteristic of the Śāvara [tradition] regarding drowsiness.
One should not perform the initiation of an animal, nor should one allow the falling of dust [upon the deity];
being composed in mind, one should worship Śiva three times a day or once a day.
One should meditate, recite mantras, and praise the Fire-god; one should not eat before Śiva.
One should not eat from a vessel made of bell-metal, and one should avoid riding in a carriage.
One should never wear a waist-cloth that has not been washed;
this applies especially on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both lunar fortnights.
One should perform worship and other rites more extensively during the [astrological] yogas and on festival days;
however, one should immediately avoid oil, meat, women, shaving, and bathing.
One should cause them to eat sacrificial porridge (caru) at night, or by means of a single meal;
for one afflicted by disease, exhausted by travel, or fearful, the vow becomes brilliantly radiant.
A person should maintain the Śaiva and other commitments according to the rules;
here, in the rite of conception, Puṣpavatī is clearly consecrated.
One should not eat on the fourth lunar day when departing, nor during the performance of a name-giving rite; likewise, one should avoid the first quarter of the month and the full moon day.
Likewise, during the piercing of the ears and in old age, one should avoid the *prāsa* and *netra* [observances];
one may eat during the *puṣpa-utsava*, as well as during periods of birth or death impurity (*sūtaka* and *mṛtaka*).
Thus ends the chapter on expiation in the Haṃsapārameśvara Mahātantra.
In the fifty-chapter *Haṃsapārameśvara-mahātantra*, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is now written down.
The consumption of mantras is proclaimed as the proper path for the twice-born;
however, O best of the twice-born, that which is thus [consecrated] should not be eaten by a Śūdra or a Sadyas.
The celibate student and the householder are proclaimed as those whose food may be eaten;
likewise, the two Śaiva teachers who bestow supreme grace upon others.
A lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) who has abandoned his vow of celibacy is unfit to be fed by Śiva;
likewise, one who possesses all virtues but bears the sectarian marks of another is never fit to be fed.

The Supreme Lord has declared that one must not eat the food of those who follow the Śaiva or Āyaṃbhava traditions, even if they abide by their own proper conduct, provided they have not been initiated.
Thus ends this expiation in the Pārameśvara [Tantra] consisting of five hundred [verses]. || 20 ||
That which is written on the heart by the supreme lord Tilaka—
whether one's own chosen *liṅga* is stolen, lost, or burnt— it remains for the possessor as the authoritative proof.
The atonement for a *tṛṇaca* [tree] that has grown again after falling to the ground through negligence, or even one trampled by cattle or camels, shall be one hundred thousand [repetitions].
Having obtained a group of ten elephants, you should make it [the object of] attainment;
that which has fallen from the hand is perfected as pure through five thousand [repetitions].
But when a liṅga measuring two cubits falls down through negligence,
then purification shall occur through one hundred thousand [repetitions], followed by the fundamental consecration again.
When the supreme, unfallen *liṅga* has been installed by grace,
they consider it a penance because the divining stick (*śalākā*) has fallen [upon it].
The *liṅga* is traditionally known to be of two kinds: stationary (*sthāvara*) and mobile (*jaṅgama*).
When it is struck or shattered, whether intentionally or unintentionally, [it must be repaired].
"There is no atonement for him," said the Blessed Lord Śiva,
"who causes the terrible destruction of a linga or who insults those who practice austerity."
O best of beings, even for Brahmā and Keśava, that [transgression] arising from a success in a hundred thousand [recitations] is declared to require expiation,
just like that of one who has dropped the ritual stick.
Seeing that the lot has fallen [upon him], the good guide should abandon that region;
for there, famine, diseases, and calamities will prevail incessantly.
In those regions, there is no prosperity, nor are the men long-lived;
there are seven physicians in the Dhara-tantra, as well as Nīlaketu.
O Brahmin, when the lot is cast, one is born [as such] without a doubt;
there is nothing superior to this for bestowing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
He is not seen at all in the world of mortals; such is my firm conviction.
For him, however, there is only purity, even when the words of his teacher are subject to censure.

Having recognized that one has produced suffering for others through the actions of speech, mind, and body out of negligence, purification is then achieved through the recitation of mantras according to one's capacity.
Having unintentionally killed a Brahmin, one should go to a cow-pen and mutter prayers;
and having unintentionally drunk liquor, one should mutter the Vāmadeva hymn in the abode of Śiva.

This rule is prescribed for all those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin). One who has killed a cow, having assumed the form of a woman, should immediately recite [the mantra] five hundred times.
Having bathed and subsisted on the five products of the cow while residing at a sacred site, one is quickly liberated from the sin of killing a cow; of this there is no doubt.
Whether by day or by night, if one sees an evil dream, one should bathe and recite [the mantra]; then one will be immediately released from that sin.
The killing of a father, a mother, a mother-in-law, or a paternal uncle,
as well as the killing of a maternal uncle, is equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
Having killed three [classes of beings] beginning with the Kṣatriya, one should perform a fast for three-quarters less than a quarter of a day;
likewise for killing a learned man, or insects, birds, and wild animals.
In that regard, one should employ the *vajrapañji* for those who fall short of a hundred [years], down to ten;
likewise for the arsonist, the poisoner, and the one who strikes with weapons.
O Brahmin, there would be no sin for us in killing one who has a weapon in hand in battle,
nor in consuming semen, urine, feces, or the contents of the intestines.
The drinking of that [liquor] at a later time is categorized as equal to the drinking of *surā*;
for all those born of the lowest castes (*antyaja*) and others, the rule should be understood as being lessened according to the degree of deficiency in their status.
"Or by not consuming food and drink; in that case, the supreme rule is superior.
Thus ends the section on expiation in the *Tilakapārameśvara*. 21.
In the *Mataṅgapārameśvara-mahātantra*, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is written:
upon touching a dog, a cat, a donkey, or the like, one should bathe.
And that which is below the navel is purified by the seven vessels through their conjunction;
just as the head, when smeared, is purified by bathing, so too is the fivefold limb of knowledge.
One hundred recitations should be performed with mantra-empowered water, or twice that amount;
if touched by one who is uninitiated, one should perform the fire-purification bath (āgneyasnāna).
One should perform the Varuṇa bath by touching the outer ear;
having performed an emission of semen, one should bathe and recite the five Brahma-mantras.
Having worshipped Caṇḍanāyaka out of desire for the *nirmālya* (remains of the offering) from Śaṅkara,
one should thereafter perform the recitation (*japa*) of the Śārṅga mantra one hundred times.
Even if one has unintentionally consumed food alone, one should recite the mantra a hundred times;
likewise, O best of sages, if a practitioner has eaten alone out of negligence.
An earthen vessel is purified by fire; indeed, purification from a doubt [of impurity] is certain.
An iron vessel is purified instantly by heating, while a stone vessel is purified by scrubbing with ash.
Cloth is purified by alkaline water; for smeared objects, by scrubbing away the smears;
a copper vessel by acid; and a bell-metal vessel by ashes.
The purification of vessels made of gold, silver, and the like is proclaimed to be by scrubbing with water; for oily objects, it is by drying them out.

Feces, urine, and recently discarded flower offerings, as well as women who have recently given birth or are menstruating, and all earthenware vessels must be abandoned due to the risk of contamination.
If one is negligent regarding the commitments (*samaya*), the recitation of the *śakti* is recommended;
however, for speech that results in a hundred unwanted insults, the fault becomes twofold.
One who has consumed what should not be eaten becomes purified by reciting the Deva-mantra along with its ancillaries (sāṅga),
having carefully considered whether it be one hundred, one thousand, or a hundred thousand times.
This very rule has been proclaimed regarding sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached;
a wise man should offer as a sacrifice his own well-earned and virtuous wealth.
An object acquired for one's livelihood should never exceed what is required for clothing, shelter, food, and so forth; one should practice the Gāyatrī mantra a hundred times.
O bull among sages, one becomes pure through the proper offering of food in rites for the gods, the fire, and the guru; one is always purified by what is right, not by what is unjust.
Whether to ascetics who are withered or diseased, one may give some medicine;
for all of them and at all times, O Queen, there is no fault in this matter within the Teaching.
If one knows that a substance— whether fat or meat— has been touched, licked, or smelled by a donkey, a camel, a cat, a jackal, or similar animals;
Purification for me is declared to be through sprinkling, washing, or the abandonment of what is defective;
likewise, purification for gold is proclaimed to be through intense heating or melting.
Furthermore, salt is purified by re-cooking it in a large quantity of water;
and even jaggery that has been spoiled is purified, O Lord, simply by sprinkling it with water.
Sweet sugarcane juice is purified by cooking;
likewise, fruits are purified by washing, and curd by inspection.
It is said that milk is purified; the remainder [of the cooking process] is beneficial when produced by boiling.
Milk is purified by sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and also by the rite of carrying fire around it (paryagnikaraṇa).
Purification from the censure of one's teacher is attained by restraining oneself for a year,
and by causing suffering to others through the actions of speech, mind, and body.
Having understood our delight, let there be purity through the recitation of the *śakti* mantra;
then, from one hundred, two hundred, or even a thousand repetitions, the wheels are set in motion.
Having informed the guru, one should perform that which is pleasing to the guru;
even what is appropriate [is determined] from the remainder. In this regard, for practitioners, the procedure is threefold according to the application of heavy or light [elements].
Everything has been explained here in its entirety; now, for the sake of the current practice, the excellent son of Śiva’s mouth is being described exactly as it is.
Thus ends the chapter on expiation in the *Matangapārameśvara-mahātantra*. 22.
The expiation for the Vārāka is now written down.
If the rule is not lost, it remains intact; if it is lost, one should fast for a day. In the case of a lapse lasting many days, one should recite the mantra for three nights.
If, due to negligence, one consumes food during the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka),
one becomes pure at that very moment by reciting the mantra of Īśāna twenty times.
If [the water] is defiled by hair, insects, or anything else,
one is released from that sin by reciting the Īśāna mantra even once.
If one eats alms-food at a single house from an excellent twice-born man,
he is not tainted by faults as many as there are morsels he consumes.
One who has been initiated should not eat garlic, nor shall he eat onions,
mushrooms, and the like, or fungi growing from the earth.
Having recited this once for Īśāna, one shall be liberated from that sin;
when one is freed from the practice of violence and endowed with the practice of proper diet.
At that time, the potter may eat from the same vessel, but not others of different castes;
likewise, if one eats from a vessel belonging to a person of the mantra-learned caste on a difficult path.
Having eaten, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times, or half of that according to one's desire;
by subsisting on alms-food alone, one is thoroughly liberated from the bondage of food.
One who eats less than once a day, observes clear conduct, and remains discreet, should recite the mantra for a day and night; thus he is liberated from defects of the mantra.
I am for a metallic vessel: copper with ash, bell-metal with alkaline water, and cloth with tannin or water used for leather.
Furthermore, one should discard an earthen vessel by means of baking it, and a wooden one immediately;
likewise, one should remove the thread [from cloth] and the like, and discard a faulty coating from an earthen vessel.
That which is of a fiery nature is purified by fire, by earth, by cow dung, or by water;
words are purified by truth, and actions performed by the virtuous are likewise purified.

And when the mind is purified everywhere, it is called "pure. When a practitioner of mantra, whether he be a teacher, a spiritual son, or anyone else, has been bitten by a dog, [he should perform the following].
If one recites [the mantra] seven times immediately after bathing, one becomes purified;
and by a single fast, one bitten by a snake is purified.
O great sage, having killed a Brahmin unintentionally or through [the force of] action, one should recite the Sadyojāta mantra therein; thereby, one is liberated from that sin.
At the confluence, in the northern enclosure, one should observe a fast for one day;
by chanting the Sadyojāta mantra there, one destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Even after killing very many [beings], a practitioner who knows mantras, who acts as a night-walker, who is impartial, and who is skilled in recitation, may especially burn away his sin.

On those days, one should perform recitation; by completing the remainder of the vow, the best of the twice-born is purified even after consuming what is forbidden to eat, whether done intentionally or unintentionally.
One should recite the mantra for the remainder of the day; thus one is liberated from sin.
A drinker of intoxicants, subsisting on the five products of the cow at night, should recite it ten hundred thousand times.
One who is constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva should recite [the mantra] for the purification of the self,
even after stealing gold, killing a cow or grain, or having slain an excellent woman.
If a mantra-practitioner has committed an act of treachery against a friend due to force or some cause,
that man should enter the water up to his knees and remain there for a full day and night.
If one recites the Vāmadeva [Sūkta] while remaining there, one is liberated from that sin;
for stealing a book, one should recite the Vakra [Sūkta] a hundred times if done unintentionally.
Having committed an act of approaching one who should not be approached, one should recite the Vāmadevya hymn a hundred times;
by reciting it over eight hundred times for a Brāhmaṇa, one is liberated from that sin.
A Kṣatriya indeed [purifies] by reciting it one hundred times, a Vaiśya by three hundred,
but a Śūdra, O Vāmadeva, by reciting it four hundred times before Śiva.
Having stayed there for one night, he is liberated from that sin;
so too is he who approaches a brahmin woman who is a woman of good family after she has gone forth as a renunciant.
Having recited the Īśāna mantra one hundred and eight times, the initiated person shall be freed from faults;
even if, through negligence, he should ever engage in sexual union with a *vṛṣalī*.
By reciting the *Īśāna* [hymn] one hundred times, one shall be liberated from that sin.
Thus ends the chapter on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) concerning the *Pārāka* penance. 23.
Now, the ancient rite of expiation for the Vidyā is written down:
"If one should transgress the rules and so forth either through ignorance or even intentionally,
O God, how may there be purification for that?"
The Lord said:

Having committed an act of disparagement against the gods, the sacred fire, the gurus, or the scriptures, one should recite the revealed scripture (Śruti), having ascertained whether the offense was minor or otherwise, with the Lord increasing the number of recitations tenfold for each successive degree of gravity.
Having performed the worship according to the rite of peace and having offered praise, one should ask for forgiveness;
that same [rite] should likewise be performed ten times for the initiated practitioners and others.
O Lord, whatever other sin has been committed, it shall be consumed by the mere remembrance [of You];
and one who is unwearied should consume the remains of the offering (nirmālya) and apply it to his face a hundred thousand times.
One should offer ten times as much as one desires to Caṇḍeśa;
having eaten, one should present the food offering (naivedya) to the Lord, and once the deity has been dismissed, [one may eat] along with one's companions.
In the same way, purity is attained by making an offering; if one has transgressed, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
Having eaten during a sacramental rite such as conception and so forth, one should repeat it one thousand times.
If one performs the nyāsa and other rites a hundred times over a bell-metal vessel during a meal,
yet eats while remaining impure from food remnants, he becomes purified by discarding that food after eating it among his equals.
For a thousand or ten thousand [repetitions], as well as for the medium and inferior [counts],
there shall be fasting for two or three nights and eating the remnants of sacrificial food (ucchiṣṭa).
Contact with the leavings of those of lower status is recorded as being tenfold [in severity];
and there is an increase in the number of recitations and fasts, starting from one night and proceeding in sequence.
If one ever eats food that has been defiled by cats or mice,
he shall be purified by bathing at the end of digestion and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

One should take cow dung with the *sadya* mantra, cow urine with the *gomatī* mantra, ghee mentally, curd with the *tāsye* mantra, and water infused with *kuśa* grass with the *iḍe* mantra; all these should be placed in the mouth.
Having set aside one side with the Gāyatrī, one should drink [water]; thus purified, one becomes cleansed of sin.
Having eaten food touched by worms, insects, and the like, one becomes pure by means of that [Gāyatrī].
Having eaten food killed by one who is excessively angry, one should fast and recite the *Narāyaṇa-mantra*;
likewise, O God, for eating garlic and similar substances, one must fast for three nights.
One who has drunk liquor ten million times shall be purified by consuming the five products of the cow at night,
remaining constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva and reciting [the mantra].
He who eats feces or urine for the sake of purification should recite [the mantra] ten times;
he who eats in a row with those of inferior status should likewise recite it ten times.
Having understood the relative gravity or lightness of what has not been mentioned regarding consumption,
one hundred repetitions of the mantra should be performed for the sake of purification— whether it be inferior, superior, or middling.
Why is it that for the lowest [level] there are one hundred and one [repetitions], and for the middle, two?
What is the highest recitation? It should be half; in the ritual action, the recitation should be threefold.
Having abandoned the *liṅga* and having killed the guru, one should mutter [the mantra] without sloth;
having eaten at night, one should perform penance before the fire, first and then the supreme triad.
By giving away one's entire possessions to a "Sarva" (the All), one is liberated from that sin;
having killed a twice-born man, one should likewise mutter that [mantra] five hundred times, free from other austerities.
Then, subsisting on alms-food, he should offer his entire being as before;
or else, according to his own capacity, he should perform the initiation that leads to liberation.
The penance is reduced by one quarter for each successive caste starting from the Kṣatriya;
however, for those of the lowest castes, it is reduced by half, and for killing a Śūdra, one should perform the vow prescribed for killing a cow.
For buffaloes, donkeys, and the like, the fee is half of that;
for dogs, jackals, deer, and so forth, the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) is half of that as well.
For killing frogs, mongooses, and the like, the performance of one foot of the penance is prescribed;
having killed small creatures, one becomes pure by performing it ten times.
Whatever sin has been committed through all forms of violence, as well as whatever else has been spoken,
the destroyer of both the terrible and the non-terrible shall consume it all by his mere remembrance.
Having approached the wife of one's guru, one should practice a hundred thousand repetitions for purification;
having drunk milk while wearing wet clothes, [one should approach] a sister born of the same womb as one's mother.
One who recites the *pitṛmābhṛt*, the *svāśveśrū*, and the *atula* mantras, etc.,
undergoes a loss of merit by the hundreds of thousands in successive order upon approaching a woman of the Brahmin or other castes.
One should recite five hundred thousand [mantras] while standing in water up to the navel for an Antyaja woman;
for a Śūdra woman, it is joined with the Sāmānya [mantra], and for each subsequent [lower caste], it is doubled again and again.
Having approached a woman born of the Vaiśya or other castes, one should go to the Ganges and recite [the mantra] ten thousand times;
for both [approaching a Śūdra woman and approaching a woman of the same caste], it is said that the number is doubled, while for goats and the like, it is half of that.
The left-hand path burns away the womb and whatever else may exist;
by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, purification occurs, and gold certainly becomes worn away.
Having stolen [these], one is purified by half that [penance]; likewise for women, goats, sheep, bell-metal, clothing, liquids, and so forth, one is purified by a single *lakṣaṇa*.
One should burn everything that has been recently produced, or anything else arising from theft;
one who is defiled by mixed impurities should mutter all the mantras for purification.
For the purification of all sins, even for Śiva who pervades the sky,
one should perform expiation after understanding the gravity or lightness of the actions.
In a matter that can be accomplished by the agent’s power, age, and wealth, purification does not depend on [the nature of the act];
for whether done through ignorance or non-ignorance, an act performed in this manner is purified.
But that which is performed out of desire or delusion is purified by the threefold [practice].
Thus has the recitation (japa) for physical [misdeeds] been described as minor, middling, and supreme.
Even for that which has been performed through ritual action, one should first recite [the mantra] starting from the beginning;
it is taught that for those who have not yet mastered it, the recitation of the previous [mantras] should proceed in sequence.
All this has been taught for the purification of the initiate who abides in equanimity,
as well as for the sake of the stability of the "spiritual sons" and others, and for the attainment of accomplishment by those who utter mantras.
For the sake of bestowing grace upon the teachers, initiation is prescribed;
or else, O best of sages, the teacher may burn away everything through initiation.
A Brahmin who has been touched by those accused of heinous crimes and the like becomes pure by bathing;
however, for one who has uttered an untruth, purity comes from washing the feet, and not otherwise.
If one who has been purified should perform the rite while in contact with the remnants of food or smears thereof,
or having accepted a gift from an unworthy person, he shall immediately purify himself again by means of twelve [repetitions].
One who collects wood for the purpose of the fire-oblation, for the sake of the teacher, or for the sake of the linga, is quickly released from sin, even if he is a despised counselor.

If that foolish person should ever eat it out of greed, he must recite one hundred thousand [mantras] and perform a quarter-penance; once he has performed the propitiatory rite, then purification shall occur.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter on expiation in the Vidyāpurāṇa.
Now, the expiation for the Raurava hell is written down.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the sequence of the initiation of the Self (ātmadīkṣā),
as it was spoken by the Supreme Lord to the high-souled Śrīkaṇṭha.

But he who, being an expert in the Śiva-sacrifice, initiates a Śūdra according to the rule for the Ugras, having consumed the remains of the offering (nirmālya) during times of distress; (p. 32a) [he incurs sin].
Having transcended the command or even the authority of the supreme lord within the teaching,
one who has properly observed the vows should perform this self-initiation according to the rule.
Thus ends this expiation for the Raurava hell. || 24 ||
In the *Mṛgendra-tattva-saṃhitā*, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is written:
"In the event of an interruption in the practice and so forth, one should recite the *sadyojāta* mantra joined [with the appropriate syllables]."
For a hundred days, with his vital breaths restrained, he subsisted on air during the day;
for in the consumption of the "left" food (vāma), there is indeed violence toward that which possesses many forms.
If the mouth quivers at night, one should perform twice as many [recitations] during the day;
due to contact with the impurities of a twice-born person, the number for clothing and other items should be increased sixfold.
In the center of the eight-petaled lotus, one should recite the fifth mantra;
for six days, one should recite it one hundred thousand times, even while subsisting on [only] grain.
One should perform ten thousand oblations and double that number of recitations to effect purification;
due to contact with the remains of offerings (nirmālya), one must recite all the Brahmāṇīs a hundred thousand times.
One should recite the complete collection one hundred thousand times while consuming the remains of offerings (nirmālya).
Vāmā and the others are the consorts of the Śākya-pādārthikas and the Kapālins.
One who has not yet attained the status of a householder should be known as the authority for those who bear the lifelong marks of asceticism;
their purity regarding food at the end of that period is like the purity resulting from the cessation of contact with a low caste.
Indeed, what is declared as the Aindava vow? The Kāpālikas and Ājīvikas are considered [born from] the mouth of Īśāna;
one should recite [the mantra of] Īśāna one hundred thousand times for the purification of that mixture.
Having reached a firm resolve regarding the three hundred thousand [recitations] for the *kāpāla-saṃkara* [offense],
one who has approached a woman through negligence should perform ten thousand breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*) and recite [the mantra].
Multiplied by ten and five (one hundred fifty), conjoined with the utterance of the *praṇava* for purification,
and joined with the eleven [recitations] of Śiva when there is a connection with a great sin (*mahāpātaka*).
One who restrains the breath and subsists on roots should mutter [the mantra] ten times;
however, when eating roots from those very same trees, one may do so even without breath control (prāṇāyāma).
In the case of sins, their consequences, and transgressions of ritual acts,
one should recite either eleven times or once the imperishable Brahman.
One should not take even a small water-pot brought by a female friend under the mistaken impression that it belongs to her;
if one takes it out of ignorance, one should perform half of the penance prescribed for such an act.
In a yoga involving many deities, the commonality [of attributes] is equal due to the nature of the yoga;
the wise man should not overstep the asterism, for it is the cause of both creation and dissolution.
Having overcome this initial fault, one should recite [the mantra] joined with many forms.
Thus ends the chapter on expiation in the Mṛgendra-tattva-saṃhitā.
The expiation for failing to perform the daily rites (*nisvāsakārikā*) is written here:
A practitioner of mantra who has not completed his daily duties should not perform any other ritual action.
In the event of an interruption of the daily rites through negligence, an oblation of clarified butter (*ghṛtahoma*) is prescribed.
One should offer a thousand oblations into the sacrificial fire with the thirty-two-syllable mantra, as many times as one is able.
Having thus performed the oblation, the mantra-practitioner should then recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
in the daily ritual, there should be a division [of the syllables] starting from the letter *a*.
The knower of mantras should perform the recitation of the *mālāmantra* twice as many times;
one bitten by a dog is purified by eight hundred recitations of the *gāyatrī*.
One bitten by a cat or a mouse is purified by [the mantra] recited seven times;
one bitten by a jackal or a wolf is purified by one hundred and eight [recitations].

Upon touching or conversing with a Caṇḍāla, one should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and recite [the mantra] with the Sadyojāta [face]; one is thereby liberated—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Having committed theft, one should mutter the *ghora* mantra; one should mutter the *tatpuruṣa* mantra slightly;
and through contact with those [sins], one should mutter the *īśāna* mantra on a mountain peak.
Copper, silver, or a vessel—taking these constitutes theft; likewise for *kaṅgu* grain, other grains, iron, or various other types of metal.
Having performed various meritorious acts and reached a definitive conclusion therein, one who steals gold shall attain purification by reciting the Aja hymn; of this there is no doubt.

By stealing half of that amount, one is purified by giving away women, horses, goats, and the like; for stealing bell-metal, clothing, liquids, and so forth, purification is achieved by giving one hundred thousand.
The Sadyojāta mantra quickly burns away [the sin], or alternatively, in the case of silver [offense];
having reviled the gods, fire, the guru, or the scriptures, one should recite it one hundred times.
Having understood the nature of the [deities] beginning with Laṅgha, and having fashioned the Lord ten times greater [than each preceding one],
one should praise them according to one's ability and ask for their forgiveness.
Whether it be ten, a hundred, or even one among the practitioners and others,
whatever other sin has been committed, their Lord shall burn it away through mere remembrance.
O Guru, having uttered slander against the preceptor as well as against Śiva,
one is thoroughly purified from such negligence by reciting the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
The preceptor, who is the Supreme Lord and complete with the limbs of Śiva’s knowledge, is to be worshipped like Śiva himself; one should not practice censure toward him.
A regular initiate (samayin), one who possesses self-control, and especially a spiritual son (putraka),
having reviled them, is purified by half of that [penance].
Even by killing those who revile Śiva, the Śiva-mantra, or a Śaiva teacher out of malice, one is not defiled by the sin of slaughter.
One should recite the Lord’s mantra one hundred times as an expiation to become purified;
having stolen the entire property of the deity, one should recite the five Brahmans in their proper sequence.

Endowed with the fivefold austerity, the mantra-practitioner, subsisting on alms or according to his own capacity, should recite the mantra five hundred times for the sake of initiation leading to nirvāṇa.
Twenty thousand, twenty thousand, and up to one hundred thousand— this is the mental practice of recitation, which is very difficult to master, reaching its ultimate limit at one hundred thousand.
Having killed a guide out of desire, one who eats [only] a hundred thousand [meals] while concentrated becomes pure after reciting eighty-one million mantras.
The section on the expiation consisting of breath-control is completed. || 27 ||
The expiation for the seven types of Vidyādharas is now written down: when a bearer of the *liṅga*— whether a Śaiva or one of another [sect]— is killed,
the practitioner of mantra should perform the expiation as spoken by the Guru and declared by Śiva.
Whether performed by six, seven, or many teachers, excluding the Guru,
it must be carried out as established by the scriptures for the purification of great sins (mahāpātaka).

One should offer eight hundred oblations into the fire of Śiva with the Aghora mantra; for the mantra practitioner, even an unoffered oblation in the fire of Śiva leads to the pacification of faults in the state of Nirvāṇa.
Thus, this is the expiation for one who possesses the vidyādharas. || 26 ||
The expiation for the Niḥśvāsottara is now written down.

A practitioner of mantra should not perform any other ritual action whatsoever until his daily rite is completed. If the daily rite is interrupted through negligence, an oblation of clarified butter is prescribed.
If one hundred oblations are offered through negligence instead of one thousand,
the mantra-practitioner should then recite the mantra fifty or twenty-five times.
Having grasped the mantra with the Vidyādhī mantra joined with the five Brahmans,
the practitioner of mantra should then perform the recitation, counting the repetitions until the prescribed number is reached.
Having performed the recitation as prescribed in the Kalpa, one should offer it to Rudra;
the practitioner who has offered the recitation to Rudra is not obstructed by the lord of obstacles.
Having gone to the ground on one's knees, one should offer the recitation (japa) to the Lord.
Thus ends the expiation (prāyaścitta) in the Niḥśvāsottara.
Now, the expiation for a thousand [transgressions] in the Śivabheda is written:
one who steals the preceptor, the deity, or his own [property] should perform the rite known as Gurvaṅga.
Meat is ten times more impure; one should not cause it to be offered even with great difficulty. For three days one should drink heated milk, and for three days one should drink heated [water].
Having drunk warm ghee for three days, one should subsist on air for three days;
this, O blessed lady, is the Taptakṛcchra penance, which destroys even the most heinous sins.
The son of a Śūdra woman becomes purified with great difficulty after three years;
the wise man should eat only one morsel at midday for each of those three days.
Again, for three days he should eat one meal a day with compassion;
for three days he should eat only at night, and for three days he should remain without food.

The performance of the *kṛcchra* penance has thus been briefly illustrated. Having committed an act of approaching one who should not be approached (*agamyā*), one should perform the *sāntapana-kṛcchra*.
Having fasted for a day and night, one should drink cow's urine, cow dung, milk, clarified butter, curd, and water boiled with kuśa grass; this is known as the Sāntapana penance.
Having killed a cow, a horse, a deer, or similar animals, a twice-born man shall perform the Prājāpatya penance;
he shall eat food obtained unasked for three days and subsist on water for three days.
One should eat a single meal for three days, and then remain without food for one day oneself.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s bed—
those men by whom these have been committed are remembered by the wise as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin).
He who possesses this [mantra] shall become equal even to those praised for their yoga;
having slain a Brahmin, he should immediately recite it while well-restrained in the midst of a cow's urine.
Having drunk liquor, one should recite the Vāmadeva mantra for purification in the temple of Śiva;
having committed an act of violence out of desire, one should recite it in the cremation ground.
In the case of approaching the wife of one's guru, or in the forest where desire arises,
one should recite [the mantra] for these [transgressions], bowing before the Lord with senses restrained.
Having made it manifest and focused one-pointedly, one becomes purified by reciting it one hundred thousand times;
even for an unintentional act in secret, purification shall come from reciting it one thousand times.
If done intentionally in secret, one should recite it twenty thousand times; if done unintentionally in public, one should likewise recite it twenty thousand times.
One who, out of lust, has sexual intercourse with the wife of his guru, the compassionate teacher should initiate him with the *kṛcchra* penance;
he becomes purified by one hundred thousand recitations.
When one has intentionally drunk liquor, he should recite the Vāmadeva mantra one thousand times.
If one recites [the mantra] three hundred times unintentionally, purification is desired;
if the consumption of the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) occurs through negligence, one should recite it ten thousand times.
Likewise, one who has taken initiation out of desire for various forms becomes purified;
one eating the food of a menstruating woman should recite the Guhyaka mantra one hundred times.
Just as one incurs five hundred [strokes] for stepping over the remains of offerings (nirmālya) out of desire, so too,
having consumed the remains of offerings belonging to Śaṅkara, one should mutter the Ghorāḥ mantra a hundred times there.
But if the floral offering (nirmālya) is neglected and consumed by crows, dogs, or other such creatures,
the mantra-practitioner becomes purified by reciting the thousand-fold Bahurūpa mantra.
Having worshipped the Guru especially on this occasion of auspicious touch, one should recite the Śivāṣṭaka one hundred times without having offered the bali there.
When one eats without having offered [the food] after worshipping Śiva, one should recite the mantra one hundred times;
[this applies when defiled by] dogs, cats, pigs, cocks, mongooses, monkeys, or roosters.
If one should touch [food] that has been touched by a vulture, a crow, or similar creatures, or if one should eat it,
one becomes pure by reciting the *Śivaikādaśikā* and consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having eaten during a period of impurity due to birth or death, one should recite the five mantras beginning with *sava* one thousand times if done intentionally,
and one hundred times if done unintentionally.

One should recite the Gaṇikānnasūkta two hundred times; for those who have fallen from their status, one should recite the Śataṃ japet [sūkta] one hundred times; or on the eighth day, one should recite the Vāmadevya Sūkta one hundred times.
Upon emerging from the seat after eating, one should recite the *vaktra* mantra a hundred times;
having eaten food on the fourth day [of the lunar cycle], one should recite the *vāmadeva* mantra a hundred times.
If one eats food that has become stale, one should recite the Aghora mantra three hundred times;
if one does so intentionally, it is said that one thousand recitations are required for consuming impure food.
After vomiting, one should bathe; after sexual intercourse, having performed the rite, one should recite the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times.

Likewise, upon the consecration of ponds, wells, tanks, and trees, as well as after the installation of a Śiva-linga, or after eating the food of those who bear other sectarian marks (aliṅgin), one should perform these rites.
Or, up until the consumption of forbidden food, or even half of that [period], if it is done unintentionally,
the practitioner of mantra should recite the Sadyojāta mantra in the event of eating such food through negligence.
And for eating food from a single source ten times,
or for abandoning the practice of begging out of negligence, one is purified from that sin by fasting.
Having accepted clothing or the four kinds of skins, the wise one should recite the mantra one hundred times. He should recite it.
Having taken curd, milk, honey, clarified butter, oil, salt, sugar, and sugarcane, one should practice [the yoga] within the stomach.
Jewels, pearls, corals, gold, and silver as well—
abounding in all kinds of grain and endowed with every type of gem.
Having taken hold of the earth, the wise one should show the upward-rising [state] to Īśāna;
[this is the remedy] for all sins indeed in the presence of Śaṅkara.
The wise man should recite the Purifiers or the fifth [mantra], the Bahurūpin;
he should recite the Vāmadeva—thus, there is no doubt that he indeed transcends duality.
Having taken a *yoni* made from *śaṅkara* wood, or ash, wood, *śṛṇā* grass, and so forth,
the wise man should recite the *Bahurūpa* mantra while wearing some cloth.
She who is initiated [into the lineage] should not revile the teacher’s son or the teacher’s wife.
Having recited the *Īśāna* mantra one hundred times, one shall then attain purification;
furthermore, having understood the [nature of] mice and [other] creatures, one should consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having performed the consecration seven times with the Sadyojāta mantra, one becomes pure;
likewise, in the case of being bitten by a dog, one should perform the ritual bath as previously described.
Having accepted an improper gift, one becomes pure by reciting the *Sadyojāta* mantra a hundred times;
upon touching a *caṇḍāla*, one should bathe and recite the *Sadyojāta* once.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one shall then attain purification;
however, he who transgresses the command of the Guru or who reviles those who have received initiation [shall not].
Having recited the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times, the knower of mantras is then purified;
upon seeing a bad dream, he should bathe and recite the Sadyojāta mantra as before.
O Vāmadeva, if one speaks a falsehood through action, thought, or even out of negligence,
one is purified from that sin by reciting [the Vāmadevya hymn] a hundred times.
If one emits semen unintentionally, one should mutter the Vāmadevya hymn two hundred times;
for one who causes an abortion, one should properly mutter the Vāmadevya hymn one hundred times.
Having stolen a cow through negligence, one should mutter the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta five hundred times each; thus one is purified by Īśāna.
Whatever evil has been conceived by the mind or committed through action, one should recite this terrible mantra seven times; then the sinner is purified.
For cutting a creeper belonging to stationary beings, one should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred times;
for anyone who steps over a crossroads, one should recite it ten times.
If one has slept during the day due to negligence, one should recite [the mantra] seven, three, or five times;
likewise, the fool who insults his guru with wicked speech and abuse.
Having observed three fasts, one should recite the Brahmaśata hymn three times;
furthermore, when one voids urine in a grove sacred to Śiva or on the courtyard of Śiva, [one must perform this].
Having fasted for each [deity], one should recite the hundredfold Brahma-mantra in sequence;
at a crossroads, at the root of a tree, or in a cremation ground, one may then recite it once.

Either naked or having bathed after initiation, one should fast and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. This is for one who has been initiated and is a devotee of Śiva, when he is censured by those who censure him, thinking him to be a slanderer.
In the presence of the guru, the gods, the fire, or learned and initiated persons,
one becomes purified from sin by reciting the Pañcamastotra one thousand times.

If one has been bitten by a snake, one becomes purified by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times and fasting; then, having performed the ritual conduct, one should not disparage others and should recite the Ghorāṣṭaśata one hundred and eight times.
In the presence of the guru, the gods, the fire, and the elders, one should avoid bathing, eating, joking, and pride; likewise, one should perform the fivefold purification.
If a practitioner speaks as a eunuch, he should recite the mantra ten times;
if he looks upon the wife of his guru with a wicked mind, he should recite it one hundred times.
If one has seen Bahurūpa naked through negligence, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred times;
having killed a boneless creature, one should indeed recite the Saṃhitā.
Having killed many birds, one should mutter that same mantra three times over;
likewise for killing a snake, a mongoose, a cat, a mongoose, a dog, a horse, or a donkey.
Having killed a camel, an elephant, a deer, or a tiger, one should recite the Īśa mantra one hundred times;
having killed a Śūdra or a woman, one should recite the Śiva mantra five hundred times.
If a Cāṇḍālinī, through ignorance, remains situated within the temple, one must recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for the sake of removing the impurity of a virtuous Śūdra.

A person who has committed an offense against an earthen vessel dedicated to the Sun should perform the Kṛcchra penance and recite [the mantra] five thousand times; thereby, he shall attain purification.
Having eaten [the food of an outcaste] unintentionally, one becomes pure by performing the Taptakṛcchra vow;
if she was eaten intentionally, he becomes pure by performing the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra.
One should recite the Vāmadeva hymn for purification, or else perform the Parāka penance once;
having understood this and then eating [the forbidden food], one thereby becomes equal to that [which was consumed].

If a washerwoman or a leather-worker is present in the temple by chance, purification from the vessels occurs through the arrival of new goods; otherwise, it requires three days or a thousand [repetitions of the rite].
If she is touched unintentionally, one should recite [the mantra] for three days after eating;
if it occurs intentionally, the rite should be performed twice as much, provided it happens through a single instance of contact.
If a union has occurred between the two even against their will, then the Cāndrāyaṇa penance must be performed; otherwise, purification does not occur at all.
A conjunction lasting many days has occurred, whether even through desire.
Then the Cāndrāyaṇa penance should be performed by Bali alone:
for half a month there should be an increase of one morsel [of food] during the bright fortnight, and one should decrease it during the dark fortnight.
The procedure for the Cāndrāyaṇa vow has been declared; and from water, indeed, [arises] that which is of the nature of impurity.
For three days one should eat only a single meal; for three days one should eat only what is unasked for;
for three days one should eat only at night; and for three days one should subsist on air alone.
Thus is the Kṛcchra penance fully described according to the rule; for the Prājāpatya, one should drink hot water for three days and subsist on milk for three days.
Having drunk ghee for three days while fasting for another three days, it is declared as the *taptakṛcchra* penance; now hear about the *parāka*.
Abstaining from food for twelve days is recorded as the procedure for the Parākalpa rite; one should never engage in sexual intercourse at any of the joints [of the lunar month] or during the day.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], the wise one, established in the vow of the Praṇava, should recite it ten thousand times;
having performed half of ten thousand at night, he should recite ten thousand during the twilight.
If one performs sexual intercourse intentionally, the wise man should perform the expiation by reciting the heart-seed mantra one hundred times, provided he does not otherwise observe celibacy.
For all householders who have been initiated into the sacrifice of Śiva,
there shall be no purification during the ten-day period of birth-impurity or likewise death-impurity.
There shall be a suspension of study for four days when [the lunar day] increases by one;
this rule applies to those established in the observances of the Samayādi and other such rites.
In matters concerning the gods, the sacred fire, and one's teacher, there must be no interruption;
therefore, one should observe celibacy, silence, patience, and moderation in food.
This terrible [state] has been fully described as having three [aspects], each characterized by five qualities:
one who abides in his own dharma, one devoted to ritual action, and one who has taken recourse to the mode of life of a knower.
One is purified from that very moment; otherwise, there is a constant loss. One should speak separately and always avoid association with such a person.
Through association with that, he would incur a connection with faults and become equal to them;
yet his purity is indeed like that of a beggar who eats the food of a devotee.

One is purified by bathing three times a day and by performing one hundred and eight recitations of the *ghora* mantra; however, for a great transgression, purification occurs separately through a period of three days.
If that [impurity] of one whose womb is full were to be purified at that very moment,
then for one known as *cūrṇada* or *sṛta*, it would occur earlier, or else the hair becomes defiled.
For those who have that period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), contact [with them] is permitted after five days;
as it is for artisans, kings, craftsmen, and royal servants.
Immediate purification is proclaimed for physicians, servants, and the like; however, there is no internal restriction for those who are unattached, such as those who subsist by fire.
When the mountain was set ablaze by the flame of the fire of Śiva’s knowledge, with his mind focused on that wisdom, the deer and elephants quickly fled.
In the same way, those who know Brahman never destroy their defects;
for they perceive the equality of all things as a means to purity, without further deliberation.
Purity is also proclaimed to arise from the abandonment of association with the tigers among sages;
the vital breaths are always purified through the power of *prāṇāyāma* performed according to rule.
Purification of the great-souled Pradhāna is declared to arise from meditation;
for the Self is purified through discernment, as stated by the Supreme Lord.
Purity of mind comes through truth; the senses are controlled by restraint (yama) and the other [yogic limbs].
Non-violence, sincerity, gentleness, celibacy, and freedom from deceit [constitute these virtues].
The five restraints (yamas) have been declared; now learn from me the observances (niyamas):
freedom from anger, devotion to the teacher, purity, cleanliness, moderation in food, and lightness of diet.
These are proclaimed as the restraints (niyamas) of the Tuṣas:
vigilance, contentment, fortitude, security, compassion, purity, and control of the senses.
Modesty, knowledge, truthfulness, and righteous anger are the characteristics of the tenfold dharma; likewise, purity of speech, purity of mind, and purity through restraint of the senses.
Compassion for all sounds is purity; the fifth is purity through water.
Self-knowledge is recorded as the sixth, which brings about the cutting off [of desire].
Medicine should always be accepted from anyone—whether from mines, from those afflicted by disease, or from ascetics; there is no fault in this according to the Teaching.
One should not abandon the remembrance of the Supreme Lord for even a single moment;
or, being pure and initiated, one should remain so for at least a single instant.
One who is purified by bathing with ten times three hundred and fifty [verses] should consume food consisting of five parts up to one hundred [repetitions].
Thereafter, having observed a fast, one should recite [the mantra] three nights long, joined with yoga;
having realized the knowledge of flight, one attains devotion to that true Viṣṇu.
Then the minister should give that to him who is clothed in the teacher’s robes;
he must certainly act accordingly, or else as spoken by the teacher.
An expiation must be performed; otherwise, there will be calamity.
Among the Brāhmaṇas and other castes, the Ghorā, Vāmā, and Jātīśā [mantras] belong to men.
"Ishana is desired as the lord and master of all the lowest-born (antyaja).
Thus ends the chapter on expiation in the section concerning the Vamadevi-vidya. || 31 ||
Now, the expiation for the first [case], which concerns the piṅgalāsana, is written: O Lord,
when the breath moves to the left in the left [nostril] and to the right in the right [nostril],
whether it be common to both or in the left or right, the expiation is now written.
And if the twilight ritual is omitted, the practitioner must perform double the number of recitations;
O auspicious lady, it has been taught that if this occurs through negligence, the recitation should be fourfold when done intentionally.
In the case of a break in the [recitation of] the six flavors (rasas) due to lack of power, one must perform four times the [usual] amount.
If there is an unequal break due to negligence, having offered oblations, one should recite two hundred [mantras].
If it is due to desire, having offered four times the [usual] oblations, one should likewise recite four times [the usual number].

If the recitation is interrupted due to negligence or carelessness, one should recite that same number [of mantras]. And if the recitation is broken intentionally, one should perform the rite four times over.
The specific [rites] have been declared as those to be performed with one's own mantras;
now I shall declare the general mantra so that the expiation may take place.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra, the wielder of the trident! Strike, strike! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Destroy, destroy! Devour all evil! Devour! * * * * *?
This Vidyā-Sāman is proclaimed for the purpose of expiation for those performing ritual acts,
when [the deity] has been neglected through negligence or when the linga is fixed or otherwise [impaired].

Having killed other humans, he sports with half of them;
likewise, he kills half of those bearing sectarian marks and those bearing the marks of Vaiṣṇavas.
There is no distinction [of mantras] when devoid of their specific characteristics; nor should one recite [the mantra] while separated from the door of the distinction.
One incurs the fault of sin by killing the perpetrator of slander against Śiva, the fire, or the Guru.
One should recite the hundred-fold mantra for crossing the shadow of one who observes the Śiva-vow;
and having killed them out of desire, one should recite the fivefold combined mantra.
If one breaks it intentionally, one should recite a million [mantras];
if through a quarrel, ten thousand; but if the linga is broken unintentionally, one should recite five million.

The recitation of mantras should be doubled when performed out of desire, but not so when authorized by one's gurus; likewise, it should be doubled for censuring ascetics and for reviling the Yoginīs.
In the case of beating women or defiling the nasal medication (nasya) of Śiva, ten thousand recitations must be performed; one who does not perform them shall become subject to obstacles.
O wise one, when a conflict arises at that time regarding the defilement of substances while the ritual circle is established, one becomes pure by means of a thousand [recitations].
Alternatively, O ascetics,
a meal should not be taken by you from anyone who has committed an offense against a guru, whether intentionally or through the influence of ignorance.
Furthermore, O Dear One, if one should perform the penance again and request that same teacher,
then the teacher must grant him a hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajapa).
If one approaches the wife of a guru out of delusion even once, he should subsequently perform the *punarādheya* rite;
having performed the *punarādheya*, he proceeds toward expiation.
A recitation of one hundred thousand [mantras] for that [deity] should also be given without conceptual distraction.
One should not abandon it out of desire or delusion; otherwise, one will undoubtedly become a denizen of hell.
No atonement has been prescribed for one who obstructs the fruit of initiation,
nor for a self-killer, a killer of a guru, or one who kills another.
Having performed the purification through grace and sought atonement,
a hundred thousand recitations of the Vidyā must be given to him by the Cumbaka.
Having diligently propitiated the guru, he deserves to undergo the consecration again,
due to the sight of blood from an error caused by [violating] the guru’s body and so forth.
If that guru is approved [by the disciple], he should recite [the mantra] one million times;
however, if he dwells in the guru’s residence, [he must do so] by not transgressing the guru’s conduct.
One who contradicts his own tradition, who is unstable yet acts as if stable,
and who is fearful of the world and his teachers— such a person should go to another teacher.
But one who has transgressed established conduct and seeks expiation should be granted the *vidyā* of one hundred thousand recitations by those learned in the scriptures.
Relying upon devotion, pure and with his mind fixed on that vow,
he should mutter in a secluded and clean place that which was previously [prescribed].
After reciting the mantra in its entirety, one should offer it to those who are performing the recitation;
food consisting of the materials prescribed for the vow should then be given to them.
If there is no food at all in the vessel for the meal, or even if there is none among them;
or else, if there is only flowers, betel, sandalwood water, or a seat.
Purification occurs through wearing [the ashes] or smearing them; furthermore, one must pay close attention to the instructions from the gurus.
One should perform the recitation according to one's capacity, and likewise maintain focused concentration.
When penances have been performed, yet one continues to act in contradiction [to the rules],
or acts according to tradition, one should practice with apprehension.
Thus ends the chapter on expiation in the Piṅgalāmata, within the first section concerning Jayadratha. 32.
In the *Svacchanda*, within the twelve-thousand-verse section on the Mantra-pīṭha, the expiation for Aghoreśvarī is written.
When the property of Devacaṇḍaguru has been consumed intentionally, one should recite [the mantra] two hundred thousand times; if unintentionally, one hundred thousand times for Bahurūpa.
By killing [an animal] possessing four or five qualities, one is purified by [giving] five;
however, in the case of a mixture [of qualities], it is half of that, and for a mere hybrid, half of that again.
Half of that [period] is spent in muttering prayers during the two nights of nourishment amidst the various mixtures;
for even among those others who are well-satisfied in their minds, there are yet more.
Purification from the repetition [of the mantra] occurs through a thousand recitations with the Aghora [mantra];
however, for those who have violated the preceptor’s bed, [the penance is] iron women glowing with the color of fire.
By retaining the breath three times here, one shall be liberated from sin;
or else, O beautiful lady, by reciting the Ghoramantra ten hundred thousand times.
By reciting one hundred thousand [times] while offering a *gaḍūka* [of water], one is purified even if acting out of desire;
by reciting seven hundred thousand [times] while performing ablutions and worship, one is purified even if acting without desire.
They both become purified of this there is no doubt— along with fifty thousand *gaḍukas*—
when a bearer of the *liṅga*, whether a Śaiva or a Vaiṣṇava, has been killed.
The practitioner of mantra should likewise perform the expiation as instructed by the guru and spoken by Śiva;
however, this may be done with six, seven, or many repetitions of the mantra by the teachers in the absence of the primary guru.
That which is established by the scriptures must be performed for the purification of great sins (mahāpātaka);
one should prescribe the sequence of penances according to the general nature of minor offenses (upapātaka).
This should be performed by oneself or by other preceptors, and not by other people;
first, one should recite [the mantra] one million times, and then offer two hundred thousand *gaḍukas*.
Morning bathing, recitation, and worship are to be performed until the recitation is completed. Upon completion, one should observe a three-day fast, as well as another three days without food.
Having performed the three "unasked" rites (*ayācita*), purification is proclaimed therein;
indeed, the *padya* rite is prescribed for the *Vimalā* [Kalpa], and likewise the *pañcārtha* for the *Kālikā*.

Then, O beloved goddess, purification occurs when one belonging to the Śaiva and other [sects] has been killed unintentionally; however, if it was done deliberately, one should perform the penance for a lower status as prescribed by the Gaḍukas.
Even he who acts out of desire is purified by performing a quarter of the penance; for one acting without desire, it is half of a quarter. May Śaṅkara protect you from this quarter-penance.
In the third or fourth [case], one should perform the penance reduced by one quarter in successive order;
for the remaining cases, their purification is declared to be by means of ten million [repetitions] plus one.

Having understood the sequence, one who bears the *śivaliṅga* should perform penance as prescribed when a Brahmin is killed; for the killing of a Brahmin by a male deity, the penance is three-quarters [of the full term], and for that by a female deity, it is half.
When a Buddhist (Bauddha) equal to a twice-born (dvija) is killed, one quarter [of the penance] is prescribed; when a Kṣapaṇaka is killed, it is likewise.
In this manner, the recitation (japa) should be performed according to the sequence of water-pots (gaḍukas).

When the penance has been performed, purification is attained for those who have desires; for those free from desire, half [the merit] is ordained. This applies to all expiations, as well as to the recitation of the *gaḍuka* mantras.
Having understood [the offense] as being either unintentional or intentional, one who associates with such a person becomes a defiler;
one who associates with a defiler in turn becomes a secondary defiler—one should prescribe the penance for one who has thus become defiled according to the sequence.
Having killed a girl who has been betrothed, the wise man should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
having fasted for three nights, he should [consume] three hundred *guḍukas* of the five products of the cow.
Having killed him, one attains purification; even by drinking [wine], if it was unintentional.
If one reviles the Teacher of the Gods (Bṛhaspati), one should, being pure, recite the mantra ten thousand times according to the scripture;
however, if a practitioner of vows is killed through anger, death does not occur [for the offender].
Upon seeing blood, a person should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times;
or, if no blood is seen, he becomes purified by one hundred thousand recitations.
But one should give one thousand jars to Śiva;
whether unintentionally or intentionally, purification shall occur in this way, O beloved, and not otherwise.
If one intentionally touches with the foot a *liṅga*, a guru, a scripture, or an image, one should perform twenty thousand recitations (*japa*) there.
If one performs six times the required number of three hundred *gaḍukas* according to one's desire, then the practitioner becomes free from fault; otherwise, he does not deserve purification.
Having unintentionally committed an offense against the teacher’s seat, vehicle, sandals,
or shoes, one becomes pure by performing a thousand circumambulations.
If the practitioner proceeds with the Aghora mantra, then purification from sin occurs.
Having violated the command of one's guru, or that of Śiva or Caṇḍeśvara,
purification is attained by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and offering eight hundred water-pots (gaḍukas).
If one recites the mantra ten thousand times without desire, one should offer three hundred *gaḍukas* to the preceptor as his fee.
If done unintentionally, it is one hundred; if done with intent, it shall be double.
Also, [the same applies for stealing] a cow, a fire, a maiden, or even a beautiful image.
If one should touch [an initiate] with the foot out of delusion, one becomes pure by [reciting the mantra] five hundred times;
likewise for insulting those who have been initiated, having acted under the sway of anger.
The mantra practitioner should recite five hundred [times] with the Aghora mantra; thus he is purified.
But having indulged in desire, O Nātha, he is purified by one hundred thousand [recitations] with the Krodha mantra.
Especially through [the repetition of] * * * * a thousand times, one becomes pure.
O beautiful one, Aghorī removes the terrible evil deeds of that person,
even if he has caused offense to his guru or has suffered through some transgression.
The practitioner must certainly perform that; otherwise, there will be bondage by the rays. Why deliberate further? No one else indeed is capable of liberation.

If, due to the absence of a guru— whether he has died or is traveling abroad— one approaches [another teacher], then, having obtained his authorization, one should perform [the rite] with fifteen [days].
The lords of guides should grant it; the wise man should perform the expiation, whether it be a thousand, half of that, or equal in weight, according to whether it is heavy or light.
It should be offered with the Aghora mantra; having performed this, one is thoroughly purified.
This applies to what is appropriate for the purpose of fire-offerings, for the sake of the guru, or for the sake of the liṅga.
If one should consume it out of greed or thirst, that person becomes defiled; he must recite the mantra one hundred thousand times plus a quarter of that amount, and then his purification will occur.
If one does so unintentionally, one may attain purification by reciting [the mantra] for three-quarters of the required time;
likewise, if one should step over the remains of offerings (nirmālya) of Śiva or step over the water-channel (praṇāla).

Having recited the mantra thirty million times, the practitioner of mantras is purified of eight hundred jars [of transgressions] through intentional acts; however, for those committed through negligence, he is purified by reciting twenty million times.
When death occurs through drowning, fire, or even by fasting, those whose vital essence (*sattva*) has not departed do not truly die; I shall now declare the purification for them.
One should recite five hundred thousand [mantras] for each jar, and then recite another five hundred thousand;
one should perform bathing and worship for him until the recitation is completed.
And for the sake of purification through desire, O beautiful one, it has been told to you:
there is no fault in falling, provided one does not ascend from that position.
Those who turn back from the path are base and have failed to renounce;
this may occur even on the great highway, and one should practice it even in a terrifying place.
If the shadow of ascetics who possess the marks of a guru is unintentionally transgressed,
the practitioner of mantra should perform one hundred atonements in sequence with the Aghora mantra.

If [the mantra] is recited out of desire, the recitation (*jāpya*) should be doubled; likewise, one should perform it in the shadow of a maiden, at a rampart, a gateway, a pillar, a cremation ground, or a crossroads.
At a crossroads, at a place where three roads meet, in the middle of a river,
at a confluence, and under a solitary tree at a junction.

One must never void excrement or urine under a single tree, near a well, or similar locations; if one does so unintentionally, one should recite the Ghorī mantra two hundred times, and three hundred times if done intentionally.
In this way, O noble one, purification from even a terrible [sin] occurs through recitation;
having caused a bound soul (*paśu*) to fall for the sake of the goal, or sometimes any ordinary living being.
One hundred and sixty recitations should be performed with common [offerings], two thousand with goats and the like;
having given the instruction to the guru, one who is pure should perform one thousand recitations.
If one does so unintentionally, purification is indeed considered to occur within another month;
the same applies to sandals, footwear, a bed, and likewise a seat.

If one spits while standing on one's feet or holds [the water] with the head out of negligence, the practitioner of mantra should recite the Aghora mantra two hundred times; if done intentionally, he should recite it sixfold.
O beautiful one, a mantra-knower who desires victory should not walk with his feet touching the ornaments on the guru’s body, nor his clothes, bed, or other belongings.

Having committed [the offense] through negligence, one is purified by two hundred [strokes]; having committed it intentionally, one should perform three times that [number] for purification. What would be the purification for him? It should be performed.

Those devoid of birth [caste] who transgress the rules of conduct regarding Śaṅkara must perform three times the prescribed rite intentionally; one who acts with defilement should perform a hundred thousand repetitions.
When he, surrounded by those two, rebukes him with disconnected words, [he should know:]
Having recited five hundred [mantras] of Aghora, one should conclude;
when [the time for] eating arrives, one should eat double [the amount].
If one kills a Brāhmaṇa who is attacking him with hostility, or who is a thief,
or who is about to kill him, he does not become a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa by that act.
If this ascetic were killed, there would be a fault even if a hundred others were slain;
for by whatever base fault one acts, the ritual becomes defiled.
Whether it be theft or a violation of conduct, one should not seize them for execution;
indeed, no punishment should be inflicted upon women or ascetics.
By killing a woman whose gender-mark (liṅga) has been altered, one becomes [guilty] as if by killing those [men] who were killed;
for one intent on expulsion, the punishment is supreme, and for a female ascetic or a maiden, it shall be a hundredfold.
Even after a thousand offenses, one should neither kill nor humiliate [the Guru];
rather, having recited the hundred-fold invocation on the seat, one should place the sandals in the presence of the Guru.
If one has sat down unintentionally, purification from that occurs through unintentional action;
however, if done intentionally, one becomes purified by reciting the Aghora mantra six times more.
If, out of malice or hatred, one utters slanderous speech against an elder or others, one should perform the expiation by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times.
Thus, the purification of the higher classes is declared to be threefold;
even after engaging in conversation with a teacher, O Rāma, one remains established in the state of the feet [of the Lord].
Then, being pure, one should recite the Aghora mantra eight thousand times;
however, for that [offense], a special salutation and a request for forgiveness must be performed.
Having performed [the rite] with such opposition, Gaya is likewise purified;
or else, it is a general summary of sins for all defects.
Having ascertained through the application of penance whether an action is light or heavy,
one should then bestow that which is established by the scriptures or that which has been spoken by the Guru.
The word of the Guru is indeed authoritative,
yet it is that which the Guru imparts to the disciple which makes one pure, O Śivā.
He too, having discerned the strength, the time, the recipient, the age, and the wealth [of the seeker], should grant it;
and for the sake of the purification of others, he should perform the beneficial practice of recitation (japa).
The affliction of the *prāra* lasts for one month, such that it does not arise for men;
this essential core of action, well-considered and concise, should be imparted.
Or else, it should be performed by others—by a brother, a sister, or even for a child—whenever there is a danger to life; thereafter, it is accomplished.
Now, for those who are aged, afflicted by diseases, or emaciated,
as well as for women, this [treatment] has been taught in brief.

For the sake of purification from a great sin (mahāpātaka), a teacher may even perform penance on behalf of another teacher; for ordinary minor sins (upapātaka), one should perform them with a conscious mind, whether awake or asleep.
Thus, whatever other sins there may be, whether mentioned or unmentioned, they must be purified through the purification of one's intention; for that which is impure is what partakes of purification.
Thus ends the chapter on expiation in the *Aghoreśvarī-svacchanda*, within the twelve-thousand-verse *Mantrapīṭha*.
Now, the expiation for the Mantrapīṭha in the *Svacchanda* is written:
42b) When a practitioner of mantra does not perform the worship for even a single day, [an expiation must be performed].
The mantra-practitioner should recite [the mantra] five hundred times, and the worship should be twofold;
as the worship is, so too the recitation is proclaimed to be twofold.
Having performed the ritual for the destruction [of obstacles], as well as for the meditative absorptions (samādhi) and likewise for the meditative states themselves,
one should perform it in my sacrifice, as well as for the practitioner (sādhaka) and the preceptor (ācārya).
O beloved, listen as I speak regarding speech, as well as anger:
one should perform two thousand recitations when an offense against the *samaya* has been committed through anger.
One should perform double [the rite] for a son, and one should recite double [the mantra] for a practitioner (sādhaka).
O Goddess, when there is an insult against the teacher (ācārya), it is double that of the practitioner.
When one who has taken a vow is struck many times with sticks and other such objects,
yet no blood is seen even though he has been beaten with numerous rods;
And two yutas, O lady of beautiful limbs, have been described by me to you;
as before, they yield double the fruit in matters concerning sons and so forth.
Though struck by thousands of weapons such as the *kṣurika* and others, including the *kulaka*, he was not overwhelmed by the blood; indeed, he survived despite extreme suffering.
Fifty lakhs have indeed been described for you, O beautiful one;
by placing [the mantra], it destroys the one bound by the pledge (samayin), and he is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
I have stated that for those who desire sons, the result is twofold;
and for the practitioner, O high-minded one, it is said to be twice that again.
O Goddess of the Gods, he who, out of delusion, kills his preceptor after having recited the Bahurūpa mantra four crores of times, shall certainly not escape this fate; it is never otherwise.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, as for anyone who, out of ignorance or delusion, should cause [the mantra] to fall,
